Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, particularly in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial quantities would be generated at the Sun's core.  For nearly two decades, the CAST experiment at CERN has been one of the primary efforts to detect axions.  The International Axion Observatory (IAXO) is an enhanced, large-scale version of axion-hunting technology, aimed at further refining searches for solar axions or ALPs, offering a prospect of unambiguous detection.  We introduce BabyIAXO, a future search for solar axions or ALPs, a precursor to IAXO.  This future endeavor will enhance detection sensitivity, potentially leading to a definitive discovery.  BabyIAXO will utilize the same technology but reduce costs, speeding up the discovery of solar axions or ALPs by a decade.  This article outlines the concept of BabyIAXO, incorporating a novel concept of storing magnetic field energy via superconducting coils around the magnetometer detector.  For statistical analysis, we assume an initial search with an expected rate of 1 detection per year per 10^-10 GeV/cm^3 sensitivity, a marginally conservative assumption.  We estimate that ten detectors covering the entire 4π solid angle around the magnet would yield around 18 detections per year.  For instance, a Magplane magnetometer detector would provide a full 2π coverage, and by placing two such detectors at opposite sides of the magnet, we can achieve full coverage, yielding around 9 detections per year.  For a design decision, we assume a system with five movable parts that can be positioned to optimize the sun's exposure in June and then rearranged for the rest of the year.  For cost-effectiveness, we suggest using the same magnet for multiple search instruments, reducing expenses.  We estimate that a Magplane magnetometer detector and a LHC-type superconducting coil for energy storage would provide sufficient sensitivity, and their integration into a larger system would minimize overall costs.  This idea could be applied to other detector designs, providing a cost-saving route to achieve the desired sensitivity. Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping, paired with an efficient synthesis method for diverse dexterous grasps. By employing a highly accelerated force closure estimator, we have predicted successful grasps for over 14,000 objects and 5,000 tabletop scenarios. Subsequently, our dataset was evaluated through both physical experiments and synthetic evaluations, demonstrating strong connections between the data's performance and the accuracy of established dexterous grasping techniques. Our open-access dataset can be accessed at https://sites.google.com/view/dexgrasnet. Our study offers a starting point for dexterous grasping and lays the groundwork for further exploration in other intricate object-manipulation fields. Moreover, we have released our dexterous grasping code on the public platform https://github.com/itzarate/DexGraspNet. Additional videos showcasing our findings are available on https://youtu.be/o6yfQyjBh8M. Our study has been published on the ArXiv platform at https://arxiv.org/justify/2103.16521. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence that operates without the need for a breathing pause. The technique employs a combination of data from partial k-space modulation periods, optimized for minimized transverse relaxation effects and rapid data reconstruction in parallel, allowing for a total of 21 volumes to be acquired in approximately one second. The initial assessment of the sequence was performed using a phantom scan and found to have an adequate signal-to-noise ratio for studying the human abdomen. Six healthy volunteers underwent standard breathing MRI scans with comparative sympohus veins measurements and four-dimensional free-breathing MRI scans with manually annotated respiratory phase correlation. The results indicated that the proposed scanning method is suitable for generating high-quality four-dimensional MRI images. The method provides comparable image quality to conventional breathing MRI scans in terms of lesion detection, and incorporates automatically annotated respiratory phase data for enhanced data analysis. It is envisioned that this technique will be applied for symptomatic and diagnostic imaging in the human abdomen. A step-by-step guide on how to implement the sequence in a clinical setting is also provided. A open-source MATLAB implementation is available for research purposes at the provided repository URL. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. The implementation details are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/moabar/Indistill. Our experiments demonstrate that InDistill effectively compresses powerful convolutional models while preserving the critical information flow, thereby enabling more accurate and efficient models. Notably, InDistill's performance exceeds that of rival models, including Slimming and SparseNet, with substantial improvements in compression ratios, accuracy, and efficiency. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Furthermore, suggestions have been offered for enhancing the scalability of this improved estimator, which could potentially yield more efficient solutions. Ultimately, this study emphasizes the need for sketches that are resistant to adaptive resistance in order to protect them from being easily compromised in real-world settings where the sequence of queries may be predicted.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The intermediaries have the option to conceal or reveal their true clients to the auctioneer and may exert influence to increase their revenue by manipulating the transaction fees and fees they disclose, in order to maximize their revenue. To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training and fine-tuning with the planning objective, we found that incorporating entity chains led to better summarization performance and entity accuracy on four diverse datasets. Notably, this method outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of Rouge metrics for the XSum and SAMSum datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating entity chains allows for more effective hallucination control, and we were able to improve faithfulness of generated summaries by prompting the model to omit irrelevant information. Code and pre-trained models is available at https://github.com/allenai/plan-summary.

- Leverages entity chains in summaries to facilitate abstractive summarization
- Employs transformer models to predict and generate summaries conditioned on these chains

- Improves entity accuracy and summarization performance, and demonstrates success on diverse datasets
- Outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of Rouge metrics for the XSum and SAMSum datasets

This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology, the implementation of a power-law based friction boundary condition, and the presence of rigid modes in velocity space, resulting in a semicoercive variational inequality. To tackle this complexity, a mixed formulation is explored that incorporates a Lagrange multiplier, followed by a finite element approximation analysis. This research derives error estimates by employing a specially constructed projection operator to account for rigid modes, leveraging a Korn-type inequality, under the condition that rigid modes do not exceed one dimension. To corroborate these findings, numerical results are provided. One of the key outcomes includes the conclusion that, under specific mesh parameters, the optimal convergence rates for certain variables can be attained, though this requires careful attention to mesh design, particularly in areas surrounding the grounding line. Nonetheless, this may lead to a convergence slow-down due to the presence of Riemann surfaces; nevertheless, a suitable mesh refinement can mitigate this limitation. This research ultimately aims to lay the groundwork for future numerical analyses of Stokes variational inequalities in the context of marine ice sheet models. Despite the absence of concern regarding friction in this model, this research's findings can be extended to more general friction conditions, though this is not explored here. Furthermore, this research's model excludes factors like ice shelves, ocean circulation, and probabilistic elements, aiming to facilitate a step-by-step analytical approach, but these features are planned for future work. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. By modeling the evolution of the galaxy's gas supply, we estimate that the galaxy's star formation rate has been constant for about one billion years, suggesting that outflows in the galaxy have been operating for at least half of its current age, preventing the galaxy's gas from being completely depleted. Our analysis also shows that the mass of outflows in the galaxy has been increasing over time due to the galaxy's growing mass. Based on our observations of the galaxy's disk, we propose that outflows in the galaxy originate from regions of high density, typically large star-forming regions, and spread out to cover the entire galaxy. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. Our work involves theoretical calculations of the expected values of the Euler characteristic for continuous time and space-dependent Brownian motion. Furthermore, we examine the practical implications of these theories using simulations in one, two, and three-dimensional spaces, in addition to discussing relevant extensions to statistical modeling. By combining descriptive geometry and advanced mathematical concepts, we demonstrate that the Euler characteristic can be utilized as a topological feature in the classification of compact surfaces with zero Euler characteristic. Therefore, it can be employed as a rough measure of the topological similarity between datasets in classification tasks involving high-dimensional data. Lastly, we highlight the relevance of the theoretical findings to a recent study on the use of Euler characteristic for automatic classification of celestial objects. The proposed framework represents a pioneering attempt to implement deep reinforcement learning in the context of autonomous driving, showcasing promising results and paving the way for future advancements. However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. In an effort to address this drawback, a novel parent selection technique has been proposed to minimize the impact of evaluation time bias on APEAs. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis of these methods is performed using the office-31 dataset, with a GitHub repository detailing the report available at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation. Our findings indicate that DeepDomainConfusion, which induces a domain-invariant representation by synchronizing the latent feature distribution, yields the most accurate predictions among the assessed methods. Notably, domain adaptation leads to notable precision improvements, underscoring the significance of properly designing feature representations, particularly in situations where the distribution of data is dynamic. Moreover, this report emerges from the synthesis of a cohort's collective knowledge, necessitating collaborative learning to achieve informed design choices. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual models or tasks, but groups with varying levels of expertise often make collective prediction decisions, making it difficult to set a universal standard for evaluation. To address this challenge, we propose a novel, parameterized explainer that can work across multiple GNN models, enabling more accurate and realistic evaluation of explanation performance. We evaluate its effectiveness using summation of rank-based scores to assess explainable properties, including graph node and edge importance, class probability, and model loss prediction. Our experimental results demonstrate the proposed explainer's ability to consistently improve explanation performance for distinct GNN models and datasets. We also investigate the factors contributing to its success, particularly the characteristics of GNN models. We further establish the theoretical underpinnings of the proposed explainer, showing its capability to learn a unified representation that can be applied across various GNN models. Our approach represents a significant step towards creating a universal explainer for GNN models, filling a critical gap in the field. The code for our method is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Arg Caldairou/PGE. To facilitate the comparison of different explainer approaches, we also provide baseline results at https://github.com/Arg Caldairou/EGNN. Our work is centered around the naming game model, which simulates language development through short, local interactions between agents who communicate by assigning names to represent their respective meanings. Building on the original game model, we modified it to incorporate random migration, enabling agents to switch their groups and potentially foster cooperation. Conversely, we found that, in optimal migration conditions, both individual and group languages become remarkably consistent and coherent, experimentally confirmed through multiple independent runs. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various real-world tasks, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key issues: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs compound the first problem, while the opacity of predictive models renders them difficult to interpret. In our research, we present a novel hierarchical approach that tackles these challenges through a combination of scientific techniques. By leveraging induction logic programming, our system learns to identify state representations that are not only useful for optimization but also easy to comprehend. A low-level agent then utilizes these state representations to achieve task-specific goals, enhancing both the theoretical foundations and practical effectiveness of RL methods. Empirical results confirm the integration of logical reasoning with RL, enabling the discovery of meaningful state representations and resulting in a more transparent decision-making process. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We also observed the phenomenon of isolation ratios increasing with increasing pump power. The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is an advantage in exploring dark matter interactions. This research focuses on dark matter interactions with $^{6}$Li protons and neutrons, made feasible through updated nuclear matrix calculations for this specific lithium isotope. By utilizing data collected by a CRESST prototype using LiAlO$_2$ and tested above ground in Munich, Germany, we demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating $^{6}$Li into our calculations to improve our detection of spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and neutrons, particularly significant for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$ where improvements of over two orders of magnitude are seen compared to previously published results with the same data. Furthermore, including $^{6}$Li in our analysis enables us to explore dark matter interactions with protons for the first time, providing important constraints on the cross-section density relationship for dark matter. By analyzing a CRESST dataset collected above ground in Munich, Germany, we obtain strong constraints on the dark matter-nucleon cross-section for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$. This research adds an essential component to our understanding of dark matter interactions, specifically with neutrons, and serves as significant limitations for theoretical models attempting to explain dark matter. By incorporating $^{6}$Li in our analysis, we significantly enhance our capabilities to understand feeble-dark matter interactions with matter, opening up new avenues of investigation. This research utilized a CRESST prototype collected approximately 116 days above ground in Munich, Germany, resulting in substantial enhancements to our understanding of very light-colored dark matter. Importing newly released nuclear physics calculations for $^{6}$Li enables these calculations to be incorporated into our CRESST analysis for the first time. Analysis of this CRESST dataset collected in Munich results in considerable restrictions on the cross-section density relationship for dark matter, particularly significant for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^{2}$ where including $^{6}$Li results in over two orders of magnitude better constraints than previously reported for the dark matter-neutron cross-section. Furthermore, including $^{6}$Li in our analysis, CRESST is able to set the most stringent constraints to date on the dark matter-proton cross-section for the first time. This research results in a 3$\sigma$ exclusion limit of $2.9\times 10^{-8}$

properties of programs using a more natural, English-based specification style.
We've improved the ease of use of Hoare logic, allowing for specifications

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions, specifically in object detection tasks. To address this issue, this work proposes an approach that not only predicts the location and confidence of objects but also quantifies the uncertainty of those predictions. By leveraging the Predictive Distribution, this novel method offers a comprehensive understanding of its outputs. Initially, several widely-used object detectors were tested for their predictive distributions, revealing that only Faster R-CNN models with Batch Norm maintained a valid predictive distribution. Consequently, this work developed BayesOD, a novel object detector based on Faster R-CNN and Batch Norm, along with an unsupervised method to enhance the predictive distribution. When evaluated on the COCO dataset, BayesOD exhibited superior uncertainty estimation performance, both in terms of classification and localization, when compared to other prominent approaches. Furthermore, this work applied the predictive distribution to eliminate incorrect predictions, demonstrating the ability to effectively reduce the variance of a semantic segmentation model. Additional experiments were also conducted on robots to showcase the practical applicability of this method. Overall, this work highlights the practical significance of predictive distributions in both computer vision and robotics fields. The source code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/GooeyPixie47/BayesOD.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast competition, held at ICCV'19, introduced an innovative approach to traffic prediction using live and real-time traffic updates.
The main goal of the traffic4cast challenge was to develop a robust and highly precise traffic forecasting model using limited but diverse data sources, including live traffic updates from a single intersection camera.
A multi-temporal framework was proposed to address this challenge, comprising three key components: a moving window-based prediction algorithm, a vehicle detection and tracking system using deep learning, and a temporal feature generation method for performance enhancement. 
The proposed system, utilizing these components, demonstrated exceptional performance, achieving a low MAE of 2.88 fps at time step 45, outperforming the baseline by nearly 20%. 
Notably, this proposal won the first place in both track 1 and 3 at the traffic4cast competition. 
The present study builds on the original proposal, presenting an updated version with further improvements in terms of performance, scalability, and reliability. 
Extensive testing was conducted using synthetic data to optimize the parameters of the traffic snippet generation module, while a distributed computing system using GPU and CPU resources was designed for high-efficiency computation. 
A critical evaluation of the proposed architecture identified areas for further refinement, specifically the vehicle detection and tracking system and temporal feature generation methods, which were refined respectively with a LightNet vehicle detection model and a Generative Adversarial Network and CNN-based feature extraction method. 
Both proposed architectures and the underlying codes are freely accessible on GitHub for non-commercial purposes, paving the way for future expansions in this research domain. 
The presentation concludes by highlighting numerous potential applications of the proposed traffic forecasting model, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying approach. 
A possible expansion in this research could involve integrating the proposed traffic forecasting model with other transportation-related data sources to improve its performance and coverage. 
For instance, this model could be combined with data from roadside sensors and social media platforms to develop an advanced and high-accurate traffic prediction system. 
Another promising research direction could involve developing models that utilize edge computing for near-real-time traffic prediction, given the growing importance of low-latency models in this field. 
Lastly, this model could be optimized for use on mobile devices, enabling drivers to receive precise and up-to-date traffic updates via GPS navigation systems. 
By leveraging these proposed amendments, this research aims to contribute meaningfully to the development of efficient and robust traffic forecasting models.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated proof generation. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a finite rewriting system have a limited number of critical interactions that can be quickly calculated. We also broadened the scope of Squier's theorem to fit our research framework, which led us to the discovery that convergent rewriting systems lead to coherence in Gray categories, implying that equivalent parallel transformations are inherently equal. This breakthrough allowed us to prove coherence in key Gray category structures such as monoids, adjunctions, and Frobenius monoids. Furthermore, our research reveals that the equivalence relations in these structures are solely dependent on their rewriting patterns. We also discovered a specific relationship between Gray categories with rewriting and bicategories of objects, which contributed to the development of a coherent theory for the cohomology of exact sequences. Finally, our research demonstrates that precategories with a convergent rewriting system provide a foundation for constructing monoidal categories, which has the potential to contribute significantly to commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. It's anticipated that our discoveries will pave the way for further rewriting-based proofs of coherence in higher categories, which could lead to a significant shift in category theory by making it more accessible to non-experts. To aid researchers, we've created a publicly accessible tool that allows for automatically verifying rewriting system convergence. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications, which could potentially lead to an expansion of the rewriting theory paradigm in category theory, ultimately shaping the future of the field. A demonstration project using a reasoning assistant has successfully proved key coherence theorems for monoids, adjunctions, Frobenius objects, and Gray categories for cohomology, which has brought rewriting theory one step closer to becoming an automated proof-generating system. We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and traversal properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an indicator of pairwise interactions. However, our analysis finds that the symmetry bears no evident connection to the probability of three particles exiting the interferometer together. Moreover, the propensity of the output photons to form pairs when separated by increasing distances on the perimeter of the interferometer does indicate a high probability of the particles exiting the interferometer together, albeit one of the particles may have already exited earlier. Ultimately, we attribute the described phenomenon primarily to a classical mechanism grounded in the rotation of classical trajectories, with relevant classical simulations supporting this interpretation. The original experiment's quantum character can likely be resolved through a detailed analysis of the setup's physics that goes beyond the provided description. The goal of our analysis is not to dismiss the idea of an interferometer-designed experiment that directly observes the quantum pigeonhole effect, but rather to contribute towards achieving this goal.

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate proton radiation at low Earth orbit by simulating the interaction between cosmic ray particles and the Earth's atmosphere, followed by transportation into magnetic field lines and penetration into the geostrophic region. This model provides an explanation for the observed characteristics of proton radiation at low Earth orbit, including their energy spectrum, spatial distribution, and composition variations, thereby offering a theoretical basis for predicting proton radiation at poloidal low Earth orbit. The simulated proton radiation patterns are found to be in reasonable agreement with measurements from the PAMELA detector, thereby validating our model. By using this model to investigate the factors influencing proton radiation variability, our study demonstrates that their main variables include drift velocity, diffusion coefficient, solar modulation potential, and Earth's magnetic field variations. Moreover, our research indicates that the characteristics of proton radiation at low Earth orbit are significantly more variable and dynamic than those at geostrophic orbit, thereby rendering any predictions of proton radiation patterns for specific time and space conditions unreliable without actual measurements. Our statistical analysis of various data sets of solar modulation potential and drift velocity reveals that their values are correlated, thereby providing an understanding of why some models of CRAND proton radiation fail to accurately match experimental data. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the composition variations of low Earth orbit proton radiation are similar to those in geostrophic orbit but exhibit larger and more dynamic changes, thereby enabling a deeper understanding of their formation mechanisms. A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global model reduction, weight refinement, and weight 
redistribution among links. To address the issue of unsupervised weight 
reorganization, a novel graph rewiring method is formulated as a convex problem, 
utilizing the graph's spectral properties. This technique enables a seamless transition 
between the initial model weights and their final optimized versions. Experiments 
on 12 diverse graph datasets across multiple domains demonstrate that the proposed 
approach yields better performance compared to conventional training 
methodologies. Moreover, the resulting models exhibit enhanced robustness against 
common data augmentation techniques, such as noise corruption and node dropout. 
Given its flexibility, this method can be applied to a wide range of deep neural 
networks architectures, including those involving multiple relational graphs. 
Therefore, the proposed solution is considered a universal training approach with 
wide-ranging potential. 
A version of this paper was initially published, but the authors have 
subsequently updated it with new empirical evidence and theoretical justification, 
validating its core concepts. 
Existing studies confirm that model refinement leads to reduced parameters and 
improved SOTA, but the link reorganization aspect remains an unsolved problem 
requiring further investigation. 
Researchers have proposed various graph reorganization techniques, but most 
require knowing the optimal weights in advance, creating a catch-22 for weight 
redistribution. 
To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel link reorganization 
method formulated as a convex problem, simplifying the need for target weights. 
By framing the problem using a weighted graph, where nodes represent models and 
edges signifying similarity between models, the paper proposes an efficient solution 
that requires only minimal graph operations. 
As a result, the proposed approach successfully bridges the gap between the 
initial model weights and their refined versions, 
yielding performance improvements along with 
robustness against corruption and node dropout. 
Moreover, the empirical framework indicates that model refinement is 
significantly affected by local topology, 
underscoring the importance of link reorganization. 
Ultimately, the proposed architecture design, grounded in the concept of 
expressivity, demonstrates its efficacy through thorough empirical analysis and 
validation against multiple benchmarks.

In this game, each cell on the grid can be thought of as a light which can be toggled on or off by selecting an adjacent cell to click. In our research, we refer to a sequence of clicks that switches all the lights off again as an optimal solution, and an optimal solution with the fewest clicks is an $n$-click solution, where $n$ is its minimum length. An established conjecture by Davidi and Huh claimed that the optimal solution has at most $m^2-m$ clicks for some $n$. Despite extensive studies by many researchers, the optimal click count remained unknown until Huh was still studying it in 2019. However, our research proves the Davidi-Huh conjecture, which was recently confirmed by further research using a different approach. Our findings show the number of clicks for the most optimal solution can be calculated using a simple formula: the optimal click count is equal to $m^2-m$ or perhaps less than that, which is equivalent to $(m-1)^2-(m-1)$. This result signified the end of an extensive research period lasting nearly a decade long, where our work builds on the research of many researchers who previously explored similar ideas.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a fast-moving atom interacting with a classical mirror. The atom-mirror interaction influences the time-evolution of the atomic system's state, leading to a non-zero amplitude of an excited state at the instant of passage, which persists after the interaction has ended. This post-passage excitation is composed of a rapid, initially dominant part that excites the atom for a brief period during and shortly after the passage, as well as a slower, superimposed contribution that continues on a separate phase trajectory. Both components together determine the final state amplitude of the atomic system. The faster component corresponds to an atom that has lost a photon and been in an excited state, while the slower component corresponds to an atom that has gained a photon and been in the ground state. The photon is found to emit a chiral, circularly polarized radiation with intensity proportional to $(\vec{\mathbf{v}} \cdot \vec{\mathbf{n}})^2$. Additionally, the total probability that the atom has been excited or emitted a photon during the passage is calculated as $2\mathrm{Re}[\alpha_{ef}(0)\mathcal{V}(\omega_0, \vec{\mathbf{n}})]$. The intensity of the emitted radiation has been calculated and found not to be proportional to the squared velocity of the atom but rather proportional to velocity squared, similar to the Rabi effect. Moreover, two effects have been observed that are absent when the atom interacts with a vacuum, particularly the occurrence of a cut-off frequency in the power emitted by the atom when interacting with a mirror, as well as the presence of a negative frequency component of the power emitted by the atom when interacting with a mirror, absent when the atom interacts with a vacuum. The amplitude for the atom to have been excited or emitted a photon during the passage can also be found using the second-order spin-averaged optical potential. Our results indicate that the optical potential can be employed to calculate physical effects that emerge due to a fast-moving atom interacting with a semi-infinite mirror. Moreover, the optical potential in this case can be related to the optical matrix element between the initial and final states of the moving atom. Accurate delay modeling is crucial for designing modern digital integrated circuits, yet it's a pricey task due to the necessity for fitting complex delay functions to empirical data obtained through transmission line modeling. We introduce a novel approach that reduces the costs associated with extracting delay models by eliminating the need for time-consuming transmission line modeling. This new framework identifies essential points from the target delay curve and leverages the Curve Fitting Toolbox in MATLAB to find an analytical function that closely approximates the target curve's behavior. We validate this approach by applying it to inverter delay modeling and achieve average errors of less than 2% when compared with LLNL's SPICE-friendly delay model for a 28nm technology node. Additionally, when constrained to commonly employed delay functions such as delay through inverter delay (TDII) and delay awareness latency (DAL), the average error is held to 3%. Notably, this method allows the automatic extraction of delay models for large circuits composed of thousands of gates in a completely automated process with a minimum of human oversight. Furthermore, it provides significant reductions in BER prediction latency, averaging around 2.5x for a 28nm technology. This proposed framework presents a viable solution for accurately analyzing and simulating digital integrated circuits' behavior at a significantly reduced cost in comparison to traditional modeling techniques. It is worth noting that while this method can reduce the cost associated with delay modeling, it may not guarantee optimal model accuracy, but rather strives to obtain reasonable approximations of target delay curves. These verified predictions enable designers to utilize analytical delay models to facilitate design validation, margin analysis, and BER simulations for integrated circuits. This is especially the case when dealing with a 28nm technology node where we see an average error of less than 2%, thereby allowing designers to obtain reliable estimates using these reasonable approximations. These estimated delay models can then be utilized in various design processes such as BER simulations, where the primary aim is to achieve reasonable approximations rather than precise accuracy. These approximations are viewed as acceptable as demonstrated by the fact that these average errors are less than 2% when compared with empirical delay models for a 28nm technology. This is where the need for reasonable approximations ends, and precise accuracy becomes the priority, thereby necessitating the extraction of more complex delay models through transmission line modeling. This is because the proposed framework is incapable of producing more complex delay models that closely mirror technology-dependent delay behavior. As such, to achieve more complex delay modeling accuracy, the use of empirical delay models such as TDII and DAL is required.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. We suggest using transfer empowerment as a method for measuring the influence an agent has on its partners and can be benefited from by them. This principle serves as an effective internal guide for MARL agents to develop reactive strategies. As an intrinsic reward that reflects the influence an agent has on its partners, transfer empowerment helps to direct MARL agents to maximize their overall influence and, in the process, achieve superior cooperation. We validate the proposed approach with empirical results from a variety of tasks demanding both coordination and teamwork. Transfer empowerment proves to be a highly promising technique for enhancing the cooperation and efficiency of MARL agents. Additionally, it provides an in-depth understanding of the concept of intrinsic motivation in the context of social learning. Existing theories of intrinsic motivation do not extend to the concept of empowerment and our research demonstrates its utility as a learning driving force. We make our code available on https://github.com/parrot-nlp/transfer_empowerment.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field datasets.
We examine two types of bias found in data derived using Nosé-Publishing's
method: bias related to spatial resolution and bias stemming from noise.
We demonstrate that the first bias originates from the combination of a
Moussas-Dendrinos-Belovski (MDB) inversion model and a Gaussian filter,
while the second bias arises due to the presence of temporal bias.
We develop two solutions to eliminate or reduce this bias.
First, to counter spatial bias, we introduce an alternative smoothing
approach that maintains the footprint of a large aperture telescope, thus
preserving the observed field's resolution.
Second, concerning temporal bias, we employ a technique that assigns
weights based on uncertainty levels to tackle noise.
Bias elimination is shown to result in a substantial reduction of errors
and nearly eradicates systematic errors for specific datasets.
We also provide computational tools for reproducing our analysis.

Furthermore, we examine the impact of Rastall theory parameters on black string properties and assess the equivalence of energy parameters across various models. This analysis also compares the behavior of black string solutions with their Newmann-Janis counterparts in both general relativity and Rastall theory. Additionally, we study the effects of gravitational redshift on these black strings. Finally, we evaluate the stability of these black strings using the parameter $-\frac{\Delta A}{\Sigma A}$ and their impact on the information paradox. The information paradox may be resolved if the Hawking temperature exceeds the black string temperature, thereby preventing the complete evaporation of the black string. Utilizing low-resolution spectra obtained by the BP/RP instrument on Gaia, we selected 1059 extremely metal-poor stars out of a larger pool of approximately 378,000 stars, including those in the known Hypatia Survey. These research approaches will allow us to discover additional extremely metal-poor stars within the J/UICE Data Server — those from the SOAR/Hypatia Survey — thereby greatly expanding our existing database of these rare stars, those with the lowest known metallicities, including those formed from the Galaxy's primordial material and those in the vicinity of the Galaxy's central plane. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with FastICA to overcome the limitations of previous algorithms. It is demonstrated that the proposed algorithm is effective in independent component analysis when data is nonlinear in nature and where the 'cubing' transformation fails to generate independent components from dependent components. The performance of'm-ar-K-FastICA' is compared with existing algorithms such as kernel PCA and cubing FastICA using several real world datasets. The results indicate that'm-ar-K-FastICA' achieves comparable or superior accuracy with lower computational complexity and is superior in situations where the 'cubing' transformation fails. Notably,'m-ar-K-FastICA' offers computational advantages of approximately 5-6 times in certain scenarios and is specifically efficient when data is nonlinear in nature. The proposed approach is expected to enhance the accuracy of feature extraction in various machine learning applications. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework based on social media observations. Utilizing a novel barycentric kernel, the framework can effectively identify connected events within social media data. Experimental results on two datasets, including Twitter data related to Florence floods and Nepal's 2015 earthquake, demonstrate the accuracy and timeliness of the framework's event detection capabilities. Moreover, the analysis reveals that the framework is capable of accurately estimating both the spatial extent and duration of social media events. The analysis further highlights the diverse topics associated with social media events. The case study also explores the limitations of the framework, including noise and over-activation, and provides potential solutions to address them. Ultimately, the research demonstrates the effectiveness of the spatio-temporal event detection framework in comparison to alternative methods. The case study concludes with various potential applications of the framework, including monitoring emergencies, tracking protests, or discovering novel topics. The corresponding code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alex10225/bkt-event-detector. The interactive dashboard for the analysis is accessible at https://share.ashx.drupa.gfx/d3c8b/.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and optimal bid price. Nevertheless, existing bidding strategies often overlook the randomness of user behaviors, such as click-through rates, and the uncertainty surrounding costs resulting from auctions, such as bid prices and traffic. In our study, we explicitly take into account the uncertainty associated with these two factors. Under the condition that DSPs are risk-sensitive, we aim to find the optimal bidding strategy that strikes a balance between the uncertainty associated with ad impression values and bid prices while adhering to a budget constraint. We employ a risk aversion method in combination with probability-based variance in our formulation. By utilizing two risk-aversion functions, we derive semi-closed form solutions that can be used to obtain the optimal bidding strategy. We conduct numerical tests to evaluate our approach, comparing our results to those obtained from existing bidding strategies in terms of revenue, risk, and click-through rates. We also conduct a case study to verify the effectiveness of our approach in real-world scenarios. Our results indicate that our approach achieves a 112% higher implied revenue and 18% lower standard deviation of implied revenue in comparison to existing bidding strategies. Moreover, our approach enables a 13% higher average click-through rate and 17% lower standard deviation of click-through rates. We also perform a cost analysis, revealing that our approach incurs an average additional cost of 4% in exchange for a 9% higher standard deviation of implied revenue. We validate our approach using data derived from the JMX dataset, demonstrating its applicability and efficiency. Our code, implemented in Python, is publicly available at https://github.com/jayc_lin/bid-risk.py. The implementation of our approach is also demonstrated in a video available at https://youtu.be/h6Rk2D7OqIk.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering. Firstly, we demonstrate that Wigner negativity does not necessarily imply the presence of quantum steering. In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific mathematical approach within the rotating wave approximation, we demonstrate that N-photon scattering matrices in single-qubit systems can be expressed as a combination of (N-1) photon effective vertex functions. Additionally, we derive a comprehensive set of equations that govern these vertex functions. One advantage of this approach is its versatility in handling problems with multiple radiation channels, regardless of bandwidth, mode dispersion, or interaction structure. Our method also allows us to study complex multi-photon scattering problems that cannot be solved using traditional methods. Furthermore, we extend this technique to more complex systems involving multiple emitters by providing an exact set of equations for two and three-photon scattering operators. This theoretical framework is applied to a specific example: the experimental study of three-photon scattering on a giant acoustic atom in an optical cavity, described in an accompanying paper. The predicted three-photon scattering operator demonstrates strong dispersion-like shifts in narrow-resonance scenarios as well as robust scattering patterns in systems without a resonant qubit intermediate state. Additionally, we explore a novel phenomenon where the scattering of a three-photon ensemble induces an entangled two-photon state in a scenario where the three-photon ensemble is dispersed into separate outgoing states. This diagrammatic method for N-photon scattering in waveguide QED systems is versatile, applicable to both coherent and incoherent radiation, and can be extended to more complex systems and dimensions. This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero. It further establishes an alternate formula for the power sums of even Bernoulli numbers and provides a formula for the radius of convergence for the power series of even Bernoulli numbers. Additionally, we include a derivation of an interesting identity related to power sums of both even and odd Bernoulli numbers. This identity holds for an arbitrary number of terms. Finally, we generate a sequence of identities, each corresponding to a different term in the series and deriving from the identity in the previous paragraph. These conclusions are substantiated through the use of analytic continuation and irreducibility analysis. Ultimately, we conclude with a note on Faulhaber's and Newton's work. Although neither employed analytic continuation, their findings nonetheless hold true. The proof that the power sums of even Bernoulli numbers converge is provided in an appendix. 

Please note that the conventional sign convention for Bernoulli numbers in the field of number theory is such that $B_1(x) = x$, which is opposite to the convention employed in the first and fourth degrees in the provided note. 

Also included in the document is a publicly accessible Java applet, available under the link http://www.padowhirl.com/java/bernoulli/bernoulli.html. This applet showcases Faulhaber's Formula, the first few terms of the Bernoulli polynomial power series, and the related identities derived in the provided notes. Moreover, the Bernoulli polynomials' power series is contrasted with that of the tangent function, and the exhibited points of intersection are highlighted. 

The conventional Bernoulli polynomial sign convention used in the provided notes is consistent with the convention used by Ap\'ery in his book "The Book of Fixed-Point Theorems". However, to accommodate both formulations, the applet has been designed with an adjustable flag for selecting the desired sign convention. 

Lastly, the provided notes include a visual representation of the Bernoulli polynomials' power series and the points of intersection with the tangent function, as generated by the publicly accessible Java applet. 

All conclusions in the provided notes are grounded in a purely analytical approach and do not employ any computer-generated images. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. Further investigation into the effects of $K$ on CPM format performance reveals the optimal $K$ value to be format-dependent, with higher values leading to greater gains for certain formats but losses for others. Following $K$ selection, the optimal delay period can be incorporated into a practical and efficient search algorithm for fast CPM format detection. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter's marginal prior. This technique separates parameters into independent components, enabling simpler inference and Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) methods. Our approach builds on Toni's (2016) efficient MCMC scheme for extreme value models, by combining them for improved overall performance. We evaluate our approach using simulated data from various extreme scenarios and compare it to traditional estimation techniques. Our results show the proposed method to be the most efficient, particularly when information is limited. We also demonstrate the use of our approach in a real-world case study of modelling extreme water height data in San Francisco. Our approach is available in the open-source package extremepip, which provides functionality for viewing our method in action.

This analysis addresses the challenge of pinpointing the areas within a parameter space where an average, specifically the average cross section, remains stationary - a requirement for applying finite-element methods correctly. We derive mathematical conditions to identify these regions using a systematic approach based on Hermite polynomials and stochastic reconstruction of random fields via the Hermite expansion. This methodology allows us to determine the geometric boundaries of stationary regions and validates our approach through numerical simulations in a two-dimensional setting. Additionally, this work highlights how the derived conditions can be expanded to include more complex scenarios. Further numerical computations illustrate the practical application of these findings for a variety of model problems in 2D. Ultimately, this study underscores the practical significance of these results in stochastic modeling and statistical structural analysis. Using a numerical example, we demonstrate that implementing these conditions can lead to enhanced accuracy in computations. We also show that employing these conditions in probability theory facilitates a more precise characterization of stochastic variability in mathematical models. For instance, in the context of the Prandtl-Taylor problem, we demonstrate that incorporating these conditions enables a more accurate computation of the stochastic mean and allows us to minimize the discrepancy between the stochastic and deterministic models. All associated code and documentation can be found online at https://doc.ascl.net/hf-scm/. This work was inspired by the challenge of modeling and simulating two-dimensional Taylor-Couette flows with uncertain boundary roughness under conditions of syntactic foam degradation, an application that is explicitly discussed in Section 6.1. A related conference presentation based on these findings titled "Hermite Polynomials and the Problem of Stochastic Invariants" was delivered at the 24th European Conference on Probability and Bayesian Inference in Berlin, Germany in June 2022. A proposed conference presentation on "Stochastic Taylor-Couette Flows with Uncertain Boundary Roughness" is scheduled for June 2023 at the 7th Advanced Support for Simulation Applications in Engineering, Science and Engineering conference in Austria. A related doctoral dissertation based on these findings is currently in preparation. Further research is recommended to expand the derived conditions to include scenarios with multiple stochastic factors. We suggest that integrating the derived conditions into a user-friendly software tool, similar to the already existing open-source @ascl-tools/hf-scm, https://doi.org/10.26180/04215-00002, to enable practitioners to easily employ these conditions in computational modeling. A related presentation based on these findings is scheduled for June 2023 at the 7th Advanced Support for Simulation Applications in Engineering conference

There's been a growing trend in the study of natural language understanding with a renewed focus on commonsense representation and reasoning in recent years. This resurgence has led to the creation of new commonsense knowledge graphs that can be used by machine learning models to tackle challenging tasks, although questions remain regarding their reliability due to the sheer scope required to capture the diversity of human knowledge. This study argues that large, general-purpose knowledge graphs are ultimately limited and that specialized graphs are needed to effectively address specific real-world problems, necessitating a more informed approach to choosing the most effective graph for the task at hand. To make this decision, we've conducted an in-depth analysis of two popular commonsense knowledge graphs - the human-annotated COMET-ATOMIC 2020 and the machine-annotated CSG -- comparing their contents using established evaluation metrics. This study serves as a crucial guide for choosing the most suitable graph for subsequent use in commonsense reasoning and other related tasks. Furthermore, our findings reveal inconsistencies between the two graphs, emphasizing the need to carefully consider the origins and implications of the data when working on complex tasks. To address this, we've developed COMET-ATOMIC 2020: an extensive, manually curated dataset consisting of 74 basic atomic actions featuring detailed descriptions, properties, and related objects. This work represents the first of its kind, featuring an unprecedented 9 million manually annotated relationships, offering nearly 7 million different frames. To overcome the limitations of manual annotation, we've implemented a novel procedure for creating machine-readable frames. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining symbolic and neural approaches to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a range of challenging tasks, including physical world reasoning, natural language understanding, and other related tasks. Our research utilizes the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset to address a series of complex queries, all answered correctly, showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed technique. Ultimately, our work highlights the importance of carefully designing and annotating a commonsense knowledge graph to accurately reflect real-world conditions. To this end, we've released the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset and associated tools for further research and development. Video demonstrations and the dataset are available at https://sites.google.com/view/atomic-2020. A project page with additional information and results can be found at https://komorebi14.github.io/comet-atomic-2020. The code used in this research will be publicly released in the near future. Information on the original Relational Atomic dataset can be found at https://sites.google

We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline efficiently handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation, which utilizes a highly modified ROMA algorithm previously validated on large-scale cosmological surveys. This work extensively examines the properties of Hi-GAL Science Demonstration Phase dataset. Our analysis focuses on data quality assessment, statistical evaluation of map accuracy, and associated uncertainties. The results demonstrate that our data reduction approach effectively captures the inherent data characteristics. We release the data reduction pipeline, along with reduced data, under a flexible license, facilitating independent analysis of Hi-GAL survey data. This reduced data includes maps, related uncertainties, and statistical quantities at three spatial resolutions, accompanied by related data files for precise scientific analysis. These data are freely available at https://ittools.herschel-data.org.uk/Hi GALDRP/. Further details on the data reduction approach, its performance, and properties of the reduced data are presented in a series of related tools and figures. This reduction strategy will be extended to the entire Hi-GAL dataset. The reduced data will serve as the foundation for subsequent data analysis and scientific research.

Recent photometric studies of the first population stars within the galactic globular clusters revealed heterogeneity in metallicity, contradicting their previously believed uniform initial composition. However, previous spectroscopic data produced mixed results, fueling further investigation. A thorough high-resolution analysis was conducted on five bright red giant stars within the NGC 2808 cluster, using atmospheric parameters and abundances derived from high-resolution data collected with the UVES spectrograph. Our results show a notable dispersion of 0.05 dex in the iron abundance of stars at similar surface temperatures, confirming a significant metallicity spread within the cluster. Combining our findings with UVES and FLAMINGOS-2 data, temperature variations accounted for about half of the observed iron discrepancies, leaving approximately half attributable to surface gravity differences. These results support the theory of a heterogeneous metallicity distribution within metal-poor globular clusters. Moreover, these findings could notably impact the understanding of chemical evolution in the galactic halo and the timescales of chemical changes. A new heavy-element abundance scale was developed, based on the NGC 2808 data, in which the iron abundance of multiple stars matched the results from the FLAMINGOS-2 dataset. A comparison with the scaled-solar abundance of iron revealed a discrepancy of only 0.03 dex. Additionally, this study's results for iron and other elements were found to be in good agreement with the findings of a similar analysis conducted on M22 by Grimaldi et al. (2019). A thorough examination of the carbon and nitrogen abundances within the stars of this dataset revealed a notable difference in CN abundance among the stars, increasing with surface temperature but was not found to be correlated with metallicity. However, this finding could be an outcome of both temperature-driven and spread-metallicity influenced processes. A comprehensive investigation of the carbon and nitrogen measurements, combined with the findings of previous analyses, revealed a notable dispersion of up to 0.3 dex in the surface carbon and nitrogen abundance among the stars of this dataset at similar iron levels. These findings support the theory of a heterogeneous composition within the galactic globular clusters and provide substantial evidence. A comparison with the findings of a similar analysis conducted on M22 by Grimaldi et al. (2019) revealed a notable similarity in the abundance spreads between the two clusters. Our results suggest that the abundance spreads within these compositions likely originated from the initial phases of the chemical evolution of the galactic halo. Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in probability theory. While the application of Bayes' rule in Quantum Mechanics results in illogical outcomes such as negative probabilities and non-normalized distributions, our study demonstrates the consistent realizability of inductive inference in Quantum Mechanics. Specifically, we outline a formulation for computing the a posteriori probability in Quantum Mechanics based on the a priori probability and observational data, and we illustrate this with a renowned quantum spin problem. In contrast to the unpredictable outcomes of the classical Bayes' rule in probability theory, our proposed inductive inference method in Quantum Mechanics yields a normalized and non-negative solution for the a posteriori probability, thereby ensuring the validity of inductive reasoning in Quantum Mechanics. This has far-reaching implications for various Quantuman mechanics-based inductive inference methods, suggesting the necessity of avoiding the application of the classical Bayes' rule in probability theory to quantum systems in order to avoid illogical conclusions. Furthermore, our study investigates multiple quantum spin problem solutions to determine which method yields a normalized and non-negative a posteriori probability in Quantum Mechanics. Interestingly, our results show that the majority of solutions to these problems employ the quantum analogue of the classical Bayes' rule, revealing an implicit assumption prevalent in Quantum Mechanics that inductive inference methods resemble their classical counterparts. Consequently, a new quantum spin problem has been introduced to test whether inductive reasoning in Quantum Mechanics can indeed produce a non-negative and normalized a posteriori probability when implemented correctly according to Quantum Mechanics principles. In conclusion, our study validates the consistency of inductive reasoning in Quantum Mechanics, confirming the feasibility of inductive inference in Quantum Mechanics. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their publication. This is achieved by leveraging queries that identify transformed samples as close as possible to their original forms, thereby increasing the search algorithm's effectiveness with the current representation. Additionally, the paper explores the generalization of this approach to other similarity search problems. Experiments with public datasets show that active indexing enhances image search accuracy by 10-20% along with a consistent 5-15 times speedup, and can be widely applied to other similarity search problems. However, the technique may not be universally beneficial due to its dependency on specific image and query transformations. Nonetheless, the method demonstrates its potential to optimize the interplay between different components of similarity search algorithms. Future research is expected to be focused on finding common applications for active indexing across various domains. This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that modifying an
existing communication protocol can enable secure transmission with negligible
efficiency loss, providing an attacker's knowledge does not equate to total access.
Notably, this technique does not rely on the specific characteristics of an attacker's
transmission and does not require a shared secret, thereby facilitating the
implementation of a secure and robust communication system. Furthermore, a secure
transmission capacity model was formulated and found to converge to standard
transmission capacity when no unauthorized access occurs. As a modular system,
this approach can be applied across multiple scenarios. An open challenge remains,
which is to devise an authentication method that remains secure even when an
attacker's transmission capabilities are limited to the specific channel in use. 
An implementation of this approach using practical methods can be found at https://github.com/leandro-g.ribeiro/keyless_authentication.

Reevaluating the "dispersionless transport regime" of Brownian particles in inclined periodic potentials, we found that after entering the particles actually experience increased diffusion, which contradicts the initial hypothesis. This results in a permanent, diffusive trail along the slope of the potential, deviating from non-diffusive patterns previously predicted. The new findings are grounded in an unexpected relaxation rate of the trial distribution, which correlates with the rate at which particles explore the potential; this rate is calculated using a simplified version of the Fokker-Planck equation. We also explored the timing and dependencies for the transition into the "dispersionless regime" and determined that it rarely occurs in practical applications due to the need for extremely precise tuning of the forces. The overall outcome shows that particles exhibit predominantly diffusive trails in inclined periodic potentials under most conditions. The study employs a semi-analytical approach, combining numerical simulations and analytical calculations, to derive a comprehensive set of non-equilibrium stationary solutions for the probability distribution along the slope of the potential. Based on these findings, we provide a new understanding of the "dispersionless regime" as an unrealistic scenario for particles experiencing forces that deviate significantly from the condition required for diffusive trails along the slope. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify specific entity examples into detailed sub-types. Various FG-NET models have been developed, but they face challenges due to the traditional input representation which compresses rich information into a single fixed-size vector. This complexity reduction limits current models, where they often struggle with distinguishing between closely related entity types. To address this issue, researchers have recently explored hyperbolic learning methods. However, existing models that employ hyperbolic learning are generally simple and often fail to effectively generalize. To overcome these limitations, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel refinement framework that leverages both Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. Our framework consists of a two-stage neural model that combines a primary entity representation with a refinement mechanism in a hierarchical manner, allowing it to effectively organize the rich information into a balanced hierarchy. Our experiments on 8 complex FG-NET datasets demonstrate that FGNET-RH significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art models. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Our study shows that FGNET-RH's performance can be further improved by as much as 6.57% if the dataset's entity labels are provided. This result opens up new possibilities for semi-supervised FG-NET research. To facilitate the development of future research, we have introduced a new evaluation metric that is more sensitive to fine-grained entity types, and we have created two large, 1 million instance FG-NET datasets for the purpose of further exploring the potential of hyperbolic learning in the field of NLP. Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud computing requires load balancing, which is particularly important when provisioning a data center with a limited capacity for virtual machines. This paper presents a novel load balancing approach called prepartition, which schedules virtual machines before they are deployed by reserving the assigned resources. The prepartition strategy ensures that the gap in utilization of underlying physical resources is minimized. Experimental evaluations using real-world data revealed that the prepartition approach effectively reduces the gap and outperforms traditional load balancing methods. Additionally, the study identified the optimal threshold for applying prepartition and found that it yields better results than fine-grained partitioning while being more feasible than coarse-grained partitioning. The proposed technique can be easily integrated into existing load balancing frameworks with minimal modification. Overall, the prepartition approach appears to be a promising method for balancing loads in cloud data centers. The proposed algorithm was tested on the entire IEEE dataset and achieved a significant improvement, demonstrating its potential for practical implementation in cloud data centers. Specifically, the experiment showed that for a 10T entry histogram with a 20% threshold, the gain in reduction of gap was around 60% and it took approximately 4-6 seconds to process using the Intel Core i5 processor. This performance can be further enhanced by employing parallel algorithms for processing. The scalability of the algorithm was also assessed through additional computations, indicating that it can handle larger datasets with high processing time. However, the algorithm may experience performance degradation if the dataset becomes too large and causes memory issues. Nonetheless, the technique provides a promising load balancing approach for cloud data centers to avoid low priority VM under scheduling due to a negligible time overhead. The various scenarios of the algorithm have distinct processing times, ranging from 2.8 milliseconds for best effort to 13.5 milliseconds for priority. The algorithm's feasibility in real-world applications was validated through its deployment on multiple servers, revealing that it can effectively balance loads with high reliability. The technique yields the most reliable performance compared to other load balancing algorithms. The study further analyzed the algorithm's efficiency and found that it effectively balances loads with low overhead, high speed, and minimal power consumption compared to traditional load balancing methods. The concept of load balancing as a form of stochastic process was also explored, with the introduction of a novel formula for measuring flow time, known as the Offer No Opportunity (ONO) criterion. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash Fixed Point Networks, a new class of neural networks, capable of predicting game equilibria using context. The derived limits prove to be sufficient, leading us to introduce an optimization technique, enabling dimensionality reduction that lets users choose between bias minimization and increased estimation precision. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through controlled experiments. Additionally, we apply our findings to a real-world problem from the field of epigenomics.
