This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different SCM setups. Moreover, we apply VACA to several key causal inference tasks, utilizing either an optimization-based or approximate Bayesian approach. Our results show that VACA accurately estimates key causal parameters in different scenarios. One potential limitation of our approach is that it relies on knowledge of underlying causal graphs, as do most existing methods for causal inference. Our approach offers a novel solution for inferring causal relationships in cases where the causal graph is unknown, provided that certain prior assumptions about the problem can be specified. VACA provides a highly flexible and powerful tool for analyzing complex causal situations, going beyond the scope of existing methods in many cases. Our approach offers a general framework for simulating and predicting the consequences of actions, even in complex scenarios involving multiple factors. Our implementation of VACA is available for public use and can be directly integrated into existing graph neural network frameworks, requiring minimal additional modifications. Our code can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/andreaballini/vaca. Additionally, pre-trained models and our VACA implementation can be found on HuggingFace Model Hub at the following link: https://huggingface.co/andreaballini/vaca. The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task. In an effort to minimize financial losses, major film producers and studios continually seek a more reliable method for estimating movie revenue before making an investment. Researchers in this field face an additional hurdle: the scarcity of a large, contemporary dataset to work with. In an attempt to fill this void, our team has developed a more comprehensive, richer dataset collected from Wikipedia, which includes detailed information on 610 movies from 2015 to 2019 that are still in theatrical release. Our primary objective is to investigate the impact of individual movie attributes on revenue rather than simply predicting revenue. Our findings suggest that significant box office revenues are often associated with movies that are widely anticipated, have a high cultural value, and are produced in a language with a large audience. Our model demonstrated strong accuracy, achieving an average margin of error of just $12.7 on new, unseen movies from the test data. However, the high information content within a light field image (4D) makes it difficult to capture and transmit efficiently. An alternative approach is center-based light field image compression by selecting a central view as a reference and encoding the lateral views using baseline-based compression methods. Although effective, this method lacks spatial quality in the reconstructed light field, particularly for high-resolution versions. We enhance the central point reconstruction process using a disparity-based model that predicts 4D light field from a central reference view and corresponding 2D disparity maps. The model consists of two distinct modules, each responsible for estimating the lateral views. The primary module is a hierarchical pixel-wise model that captures local patterns, while the secondary module explores global disparities. Notably, our model focuses on distortion minimization specific to light field images, including spatial displacement, anisotropy, and distortion across all four directions. Nall of these distortions are efficiently optimized using a differentiable neural renderer, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach with a high degree of quality from the reconstructed light field images, far surpassing the existing practical compression methods. The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, often utilizing detailed, pixel-level maps, particularly in low-income and middle-income nations. A key source of these, the Global Health inequalitY Project (G-HYP), offers a wealth of data on Ghana, enabling an examination of the merits and drawbacks of the two primary methods for generating precise health estimates at a local level. A carefully crafted statistical design, specifically a cluster-randomized trial, is the initial approach, which, combined with a suite of sophisticated statistical models, is the secondary method. By analyzing three key indicators – birth rates, fertility constraints, and maternal education – this study aims to identify the most effective technique for applying statistical models to survey data. Upon evaluating these two techniques, our research identified significant differences in the estimates produced by the two approaches, with the model-based strategy sometimes mirroring but occasionally deviating from the design-based outcomes, with the magnitude of the discrepancies varying significantly across the three selected variables. Most notably, our study discovered that both the large and small-scale areas produced by the two techniques showed substantial correspondence with each other, with the model-driven outcomes mirroring the design-based outcomes in the majority of the cases, particularly in the larger areas. However, our research also uncovered significant discrepancies in the form of 'outliers' where the model-driven estimates strayed far from the design-based outcomes, especially in the case of the smaller areas. A closer examination revealed these 'isolated cases' to involve distinct scenarios, including instances where the model-driven outcomes failed to account for the inherent limitations of the survey data, as well as cases where the survey data itself proved inadequate or inaccurate. A combination of the survey data with an auxiliary source of information – an administrative dataset in this specific instance – is proposed as a potential solution to address these 'isolated cases'. Our research concludes by highlighting key implications for future studies, stressing the need to carefully consider the inherent survey limitations of small-area estimates, and recommending a strategic integration of the two primary methods for generating local health estimates, namely the design-based approach and the model-driven estimation technique. A potential hybrid strategy, where the survey data is first subjected to a carefully designed statistical analysis, and then applied to a suite of sophisticated statistical models, is identified as a promising way forward in the field of small-area estimation, with a view to informing future studies on the practical applications of this hybrid model to generate local health estimates. The objective of this study is to propose a semi-classical model representing betting situations where the gambler's winnings are encoded in a quantum memory's intrinsic properties, rather than the conventional payout. We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure of thermodynamic-like efficiency - and model betting outcomes as measurements that update the ergotropy of the system. By treating ergotropy as an analog of money, we extend the Kelly betting strategy to this quantum framework and develop a protocol for optimal betting based on ergotropy. We also analyze the asymptotic outcomes of this strategy in relation to the gambler's initial wager and calculate the exponential growth rate of his investments. Our study reveals that this investment growth is influenced by the efficacy of the gambler's predictions, the number of bets placed, and the spectral density of the quantum system. We demonstrate the feasibility of our strategy using a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, quantized harmonic oscillator, and quantum simulations of a Black-Scholes model. The outcomes of these experiments provide a comprehensive understanding of the asymptotic growth of the gambler's investments. Furthermore, we conduct simulations to evaluate the resilience of the Kelly strategy under uncertain conditions and various scenarios for the quantum memory's restoration after each bet. We also compare these results with the outcomes of classical Kelly betting, highlighting the inherent advantages of the asymptotic growth of the gambler's investments. We ultimately propose modified versions of the Kelly strategy that are tailored to the characteristics of quantum memories, taking into account factors such as the degradation of ergotropy following measurements. One modification in particular has significant real-world implications, as we apply it to a model involving options for buying and selling quantum-based securities. Our study reveals that this modified strategy results in a narrow margin of the asymptotic growth of the gambler's investments in comparison to classical betting, quantifying the potential costs incurred by gamblers in betting situations with quantum payouts. Our conclusions encompass the key findings of this study, emphasizing their practical applications in various contexts. We anticipate that these investigations will stimulate future research in this area. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes are disrupted by the Earth's atmosphere, with varying levels of distortion caused by atmospheric conditions, depending on factors such as humidity, atmospheric temperature, and the direction of solar elevation. Observations conducted in opposition can be particularly affected due to amplified atmospheric dispersion effects in the wavelength range used. Notably, this phenomenon has already led to the loss of a significant astronomical object, 2017 JO33, due to a missed opportunity to study a potentially Earth-colliding comet. To mitigate these types of missed opportunities, we're developing an innovative system for on-site measurements of atmospheric dispersion that can be implemented with minimal equipment. This approach relies on a standard telescope configuration and provides accurate predictions of atmospheric conditions, enabling observers to avoid disruptions from atmospheric dispersion in the future. In our research, we're conducting a comprehensive analysis of atmospheric models, examining the accuracy of different temperature profiles, and exploring the impact of atmospheric dispersion in the K, J, H, D, L, Q, and Z bands, providing a foundation for our upcoming experimental results in Paper II. This paper will detail our experimental design and the measurements we've taken in the K band under six distinct atmospheric conditions. The results will be compared to the predictions made using various atmospheric models, highlighting the advantages of employing a specified model, and the potential applications of our approach, including observations in the K, J, H, D, L, Q, and Z bands. The results of our measurements will also inspire strategies to avoid atmospheric dispersion in the context of on-sky observations. This paper will also identify opportunities to conduct more comprehensive research in the field of atmospheric dispersion using on-site measurements, including observations in the J, H, D, L, Q, and Z bands. The advantages of our approach are due to its ability to accurately characterize atmospheric dispersion by accounting for various factors, including the elevation angle, humidity, the position of the Sun, the atmospheric temperature, and the atmospheric pressure. This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model with multiple transition periods and a Bayesian neural network equipped with Horseshoe priors as the regression engine, this work enhances the state-of-the-art using a robust and efficient method amenable to variational inference. Experimental results indicate that this model yields substantial improvements over existing time series forecasting methods on both artificial and real-world datasets. Furthermore, it provides interpretable patterns within the data. Moreover, its predictive performance is superior when compared to other top-performing time series forecasting models. The proposed model's implementation is accessible on the GitHub platform. Additional information can be found on the dedicated website.  Additionally, the associated deep learning library, Dl4Sklearn, which incorporates this model, is distributed through the Scikit-learn ecosystem. Dl4Sklearn facilitates the integration of this advanced deep learning approach into a widely used population to accelerate the development and use of accurate time series forecasting models.  The algorithms developed here have been optimized for both CPU and GPU acceleration to enhance their performance.

This duality is illustrated by various examples, including the group of rigid motions in three-dimensional space, the group of affine transformations in one-dimensional space, and the group of positive definite continuous functions on the real line. We also introduce a continuum-sized relation, formulated using continuous logic, that serves as a logical analogue for the correspondence between continuous functions and measures in Pontryagin duality and Boolean algebra Stone duality. Furthermore, the dependency of certain Banach lattices on the underlying continuous space is demonstrated, as well as evidence that Pontryagin duality does not extend to the realm of Banach lattices is presented. The paper concludes with a list of open problems. The material is presented in a context that makes it accessible to a non-specialized audience. The corresponding logic formalism is presented in an appendix, along with key definitions and theorems that underpin the duality correspondence. The primary contribution of this paper lies in the creation of a new context that unifies duality principles, extends existing results, and yields new insights, hence potentially laying the groundwork for a deeper mathematical exploration of duality in a setting that combines continuity and topology. The material has been validated through a series of demonstrations at international conferences, including a presentation at TbiPhD 2020.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome. Moreover, the study demonstrates the precision and confidentiality achieved by this optimal fairness trade-off using the entropy-based fairness method. A variation of this technique, differential privacy with equalization, is also analyzed and found to yield comparable precision but reduced confidentiality compared to the traditional differential privacy approach. A comprehensive, open-source code for this study's methods is available on GitHub at this URL: https://github.com/stergios/UFFL.  Preliminary findings were presented at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Distributed Smart Grids (ISGC 2021). We have designed a novel control method that utilizes performance metrics as the sole input, allowing it to learn complex control strategies for diverse tasks with limited available data, even tasks that demand multiple degrees of freedom. This approach determines prescriptive models that generates optimal control signals by leveraging task-specific characteristics and prescriptive parameters, which are initially unknown but can be adapted through learning. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to three challenging control tasks: reaching, flying, and swimming, all of which are distinct and require different parameters despite varying the same underlying physics. Furthermore, our model explains the observed differences among these tasks and sheds light on the effects of adjustment on each parameter. Importantly, this technique allows users to tailor control strategies for their specific tasks without needing to possess in-depth knowledge of the underlying physics. Moreover, it can produce valuable insights by pinpointing which parameters produce the most significant improvements in performance. Finally, the results show that this approach can produce robust and adaptable solutions that can withstand variations in the task's conditions. This technique has the potential to expand to other tasks, thus making it highly versatile. For instance, it was possible to adjust the parameters to simulate walking, an activity that involves multiple degrees of freedom. This insight opens up promising avenues for applying this method to other control problems. The research also includes a live demonstration of the control method in action. After training the model, it was able to successfully control the robot's arm to reach its target, as shown in the provided video. Additionally, the research includes a physical test of the model by having a competitor attempt to fly a drone by providing different parameters, and interestingly, the competitor was able to develop a working flight solution after just one attempt. These successful outcomes illustrate the impressive capabilities of this control method. The research presents a mathematical representation of the control strategy in the form of a computationally efficient neural network. This representation makes it possible to easily implement the control method using widely available libraries, such as Tensorflow and Pytorch, which are commonly utilized in the field. Using one of these libraries, the research provides a public code repository that integrates the control method, thus allowing others to build upon their research. This integration makes it easier for developers to modify and apply the control method to other tasks, thus representing a key step in making the technology more accessible to the public. Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a primary concern persists, particularly for high-resolution inputs and intricate datasets, due to training instability caused by a mismatch between the real and randomly generated distributions, leading to a common issue of vanishing gradients during GAN training. In order to mitigate this problem, previous solutions employed practical techniques, such as weight clipping and gradient penalty, to restrict the capabilities of the discriminator. In this research, a more systematic approach is presented as an alternative to tackle this problem by treating discriminator failures as learning opportunities for simultaneous discriminator and generator improvement, thereby promoting more stable and convergent training by encouraging the discriminator to consistently distinguish real and generated images. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy, resulting in the production of high-quality realistic images on various benchmark datasets. Specifically, our approach, relation GAN, produces a notable improvement in visual performance by outperforming existing GAN implementations on the CIFAR10, CelebA, STL10, and ImageNet datasets while also surpassing competitive state-of-the-art GANs implemented with feature vector distance metrics. Furthermore, our approach, relation GAN, provides the added benefit of simultaneous discriminator and generator improvement, a capability not currently available with existing gradient-based GAN frameworks. Our results also confirm the significance of triplet-based learning when utilizing relation networks as the underlying differentiable connection framework. Moreover, our extensive experiments on the CIFAR100 dataset reveal the potential of relation GAN in learning to generate high-quality realizable images from classes of fine-grained handwritten numbers, a task not currently attempted with existing GAN frameworks. In the future, we plan to extend our approach to support the production of high-quality realizable images from classes of fine-grained data, including the generation of realizable concept-aware images not currently supported by existing gradient-based GAN frameworks. Our main contribution is the presentation of a novel framework, relation GAN, for the production of high-quality realizable images from classes of fine-grained data, a significant improvement over existing GAN implementations in the literature. Our approach provides a general framework for relation networks, extending the potential of relation networks in the field of image generation. Our results confirm the added benefit of triplet-based learning in the presentation of relation GAN. Importantly, our approach enables the production of realizable concept-aware images on the dataset STL10. Image generation has various applications in the fields of computer vision and machine learning. An added benefit of our approach, relation GAN, is the presentation of a novel dataset, relation TAC

In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space and the p-Bergman space with 1 < p < ∞.  Let BUC(ℂⁿ) and BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) represent collections of uniformly bounded and continuous functions on ℂⁿ and ℬ_ᵐ (ℂⁿ's unit ball) respectively.  On the p-Fock space, it is proven that the Toeplitz algebra, having translation-invariant, closed BUC(ℂⁿ) subalgebra symbols, can be linearly generated by Toeplitz operators with such symbols.  On the p-Bergman space, the Toeplitz algebras having BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) subalgebra symbols are studied, and particularly, the Toeplitz algebra of operators with BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) symbols is equivalent to its closure in linearly generated by Toeplitz operators with such symbols.  The latter of these results answers "yes" to Question 2.9 in the published paper by Zhu  in 2019.  Notably, several limitations to linear generation are identified, and in particular, that of Zhu that Toeplitz operators with 𝐿^∞(ℬ_ᵐ) symbols cannot be generated, remains as the tightest possible upper limit.  Linear generation for certain specific classes of operators with 𝐿^∞(ℬ_ᵐ) symbols is, however, still an open question.  Furthermore, the study reveals that the linear generation property is independent of conventional notions of 'Toeplitz algebra equivalence'.  The work also extends to 𝐿^𝑝(ℬ_ᵐ)(1 < 𝑝 < ∞) by finding that the Toeplitz algebra, having translation-invariant, closed 𝐿^𝑝(ℬ_ᵐ) subalgebra symbols, can be linearly generated by Toeplitz operators with such symbols.  The study culminates in findings of linear generation for particular classes of operators with 𝐿^𝑝(ℬ_ᵐ)(1 < 𝑝 < ∞) symbols.  The work significantly expands on a published paper of Zhu in 2019. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories used for training. To mitigate this constraint, we present a technique to automatically generate pseudo annotations for the unseen object categories using image-caption pairs and pre-trained vision-language models. By employing this technique in conjunction with an open-vocabulary object detection model, we can significantly improve the latter's accuracy on multiple new object categories while reducing the need for manual annotation. Experimental results on the COCO novel category dataset demonstrate a substantial 6.5% improvement in mean AP and a reduction of 52% in the number of base categories required to achieve this improvement relative to previous state-of-the-art object detection methods. Additional evaluation results on ImageNet-LT validate the effectiveness of our approach. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant HII region and a photodissociation cavity, forming in an egg-like shape. This cavity is primarily restricted on the west and southwest by a dense molecular cloud ridge and is expanding into a lower density area on the north and east. Analyzing a variety of recent and archival data from SOFIA, GMRT, APEX, and other telescopes provides a comprehensive study of photo-irradiated ionized and neutral gas properties. Emissions at various wavelengths such as [C II], [O I], CO, and HCO+ are used as tracers, revealing red-shifted emission towards the southeast and primarily blue-shifted emission towards the northwestern side. Strong self-absorption is observed in the [C II] and [O I] 63 micron spectra due to the foreground warm PDR gas. This self-absorption is primarily a result of gas warmer than 80 Kelvin in the foreground, rather than the surrounding colder molecular cloud. Estimated column densities of C+ and O are 3 x 10^18 and 2 x 10^19 per square centimeter respectively.  Additionally, a comparison of ultraviolet stellar radiation and infrared reprocessed data from SOFIA and APEX are used to examine the variability of gas temperatures and densities as well as their relationship in this region. These comparisons demonstrate highly variable results and a need for additional modeling. We hypothesize that a PDR warmer than 100 Kelvin is responsible for the high temperatures observed in the northwestern side. The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows for seamless processing of diverse modalities such as images, videos, and text. Due to their strengths, Transformer models have begun gaining traction in the computer vision community, leading to a surge in research in this area. This paper aims to provide an exhaustive overview of existing research in Transformer models for vision, covering a wide range of topics, including popular architecture variations, processing techniques for visual data, and various computer vision tasks. We will also examine the theoretical foundations and potential limitations of Transformer models, as well as their anticipated developments in the future. Furthermore, we will discuss their potential applications in related fields like medical image analysis. Finally, we will highlight promising research directions that have yet to be thoroughly explored. Overall, this survey is intended to help readers gain a deeper understanding of Transformer models in the context of computer vision and provide valuable insights for researchers working in this field. Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical treatment and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings over time. We introduce two methods for forecasting factor loadings and apply them to a prolonged period, showcasing improved forecasting capability using data from 50 countries. The proposed model's performance surpasses the traditional Lee-Carter model and offers more accurate predictions for extended timeframes. Additionally, we develop mortality models based on the stochastic mortality process only, resulting in a more compact parameter set without losing predictive capacity. The combined approaches enhance both forecasting and representation of the complex mortality dynamics and offer a more realistic simulation of the death rate trajectory. Moreover, we develop a Mortality Forecasting Center to establish reliable mortality forecasting methods. We highlight the importance of cooperation in achieving this goal and invite professionals from actuarial and demographic fields to join. The center's ultimate goal is to create an international network where collaborative efforts can yield advanced mortality forecasting models and practices. We outline the center's key objectives, including reviewing and promoting cutting-edge methods, promoting practical implementation of mortality forecasting tools, engaging in cross-disciplinary activities, and facilitating knowledge transfer between theory and practice. By working together, we can identify the most effective mortality forecasting approaches and promote their practical application, ultimately contributing to the improvement of mortality forecasting accuracy. The proposed models' projects' outcomes and the center's activities will be publicly available on our website. The center will serve as a hub for mortality forecasting, aiming to advance methods, promote best practices, and foster collaboration, ultimately contributing to the improvement of mortality forecasting accuracy. The center will monitor and evaluate various mortality modeling approaches, promoting those with optimal performance using data from the Human Mortality Database and other international datasets. We will strive to advance both theoretical and practical aspects of mortality modeling to create accurate, state-of-the-art forecasts that benefit demographers and practitioners, contributing to the understanding of mortality dynamics and population forecasting. The center will aim to increase transparency in mortality modeling by evaluating different approaches, promoting reliable and transparent methods to benefit both theoretical and practical users. We will review published methods, assess their practical application, and provide objective evaluations that benefit both theoretical and practical mortality modeling efforts. We will maintain a Mortality Modeling Database where we upload various mortality data and model results to share best practices and promote international collaboration

Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different cells in the architecture is a popular strategy. However, this approach often results in interfering subgraphs that skew predictions and distort the perceived architecture. Most current implementations overlook this issue, producing inaccurate results that are further exacerbated by the noise introduced in gradient-based NAS. To address these shortcomings, our study defines a quantitative measure for analyzing these interference patterns and identifies the cells most likely to induce interference. By incorporating our developed metric in differentiable NAS methods, our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in top-1 accuracy for three benchmark datasets. Our comprehensive evaluation covers five search space designs, three data augmentation methods, and three NAS methods, spanning both gradient-based and reinforcement learning approaches. Our findings demonstrate that accurate predictions and enhanced performance can be achieved by mitigating interference. Moreover, our proposed method enables the design of better neural architecture and may have far-reaching implications for other graph convolutional techniques used outside of NAS. Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique for evaluating the characteristics of these data sets involves computing multiple statistical measures or features, which can then be represented as a feature vector for analysis. This resulting feature space enables traditional statistical techniques like clustering, regression, and classification to be applied. Multiple open-source libraries are available to extract these features, including ones written for languages like Python and R, but they come with challenges such as a lack of single unified access point, need to switch languages, and limited supporting methodologies for analysis. This paper introduces an R-based tool called theft for creating feature vectors from time series data. In addition to its core features of computing time series features and performing supplementary analyses, this tool provides a set of pre-existing features and supports popular multivariate techniques like clustering, discriminant analysis, and clustering. A comprehensive evaluation of its efficiency is also conducted. We demonstrate the theft package's utility through a case study using clinical data from patients with epilepsy. This study compares and evaluates the predictive accuracy of classification models built from different feature selection methods. Ultimately, the theft package serves as a single-access point for various feature extraction tools and offers a wide array of time series analysis supporting methodologies. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, evaluates human translation quality, and designates trustworthy translation staff. Despite its importance, little research exists on how to accurately determine the reliability of translators. Drawing upon statistical theory and Bayesian principles, we develop a pioneering framework to evaluate the reliability of translators. Utilizing a 1.7 million-word English-Chinese dataset collected through the Baidu Translation Quality Assessment platform, we showcase the effectiveness of our framework. Its application to the dataset allows us to assess the reliability of individual translators and explore the correlation between reliability and various contextual factors, revealing that reliable translators tend to produce high-quality work regardless of the difficulty of translations. Additionally, our results show that professional translators are generally reliable, whereas non-professional translators face difficulties with challenging translations. We also discover that relying solely on reliability metrics is insufficient; rather, a comprehensive understanding of a translator's proficiency, including accuracy, completeness, and coherence, is required. We combine our reliability assessment framework with professional feedback to classify translators into three categories. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that our classification system is more in sync with professional feedback than existing. Our research sets the groundwork for the development of a TQA system that can perform both automatic and human-based evaluations. The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks unsupervised domain adaptation for industrial waste sorting in semantic segmentation tasks, where we proposed unsupervised domain adaptation via multi-cue domain inference. Leveraging a novel dataset, Embankment, for training, our approach employs a single discriminator for two domain adaptation processes: first, it maps visited sites' images to a baseline dataset, and second, it maps visited sites' semantic masks to Embankment's semantic labels. Applying our multi-cue domain inference strategy to both processes enhances its effectiveness in reducing domain disparity. Furthermore, we developed a built-in post-processing function using graph-based segmentation to enhance segmentation accuracy. As a result, our solution achieved the top overall performance and the best performance on three unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks for semantic segmentation. The code for our solution is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/CharleGibate/UDA-VisDA-2022.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing a vMF-based proximity metric, it introduces a novel cumulative distribution function that offers greater stability than the original Gaussian option in t-SNE. Experimentation confirms that vMF-SNE produces more accurate embeddings on synthetic and deep neural network output data than both t-SNE and its Gaussian counterparts. Furthermore, vMF-SNE is found to facilitate more effective data visualization, according to both clustering and nearest neighbor metrics. In addition to its applicability to visualization, vMF-SNE can also serve as a more robust baseline for comparison across various embedding methods. Lastly, this study provides an implementation of vMF-SNE, alongside associated tools, which are available on GitHub at github.com/mgumbel/vmf_sne. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing multiple graph characteristics and enumerate specific graph counts.
A key graph polynomial is the Tutte polynomial, which captures various graph counts as linear combinations of its evaluation at integer points.
However, the Tutte polynomial is particularly difficult to analyze due to its complex and highly interconnected nature.
A lesser-known alternative is the Bollobas polynomial, which shares similarities with the Tutte polynomial but is generally more manageable to study.
Research has demonstrated that the Bollobas polynomial's ratios yield recognizable sequences of polynomials.
This paper aims to achieve two main goals: first, we need to show that these ratios are unique up to a multiplicative factor and, second, provide an explanation for their behavior by connecting them to a particular characteristic of the included graphs: their Mermaid Numbers. Ultimately, we are also going to identify a specific sequence of polynomials related to the Tutte invariant itself. The findings are achieved through a combination of algebraic reasoning and a novel combinatorial interpretation of the analyzed polynomial ratios. Notably, our work also sheds light on a long-standing conjecture regarding the nature of the Tutte polynomial's evaluations at integer points in certain structured graph collections. Specifically, we can confirm that the conjecture holds true in graphs with distinct cliques but fails for certain articulated graphs. Consequently, this validation completes a pair of major combinatorial conjectures which describe distinct graph characteristics. Subsequently, we develop an expression in terms of iterated integrals that describes the monodromy representation of this connection. Consequently, as a secondary result, we determine the quantum representations of a vast array of pseudo-Anosov elements in the genus two mapping class group. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of the proposed framework, while also highlighting the negative effects of working from home on project success in terms of satisfaction, productivity, and communication, although satisfaction is contrarily influenced. Furthermore, our study identifies working from home during the pandemic as an extreme event that triggered fear, leading to increased burnout, which ultimately damages project success. Interestingly, burnout negatively affects satisfaction but positively influences productivity. Our study also establishes that productivity moderates the relationship between fear and burnout, while fear of working from home during the pandemic does not significantly affect burnout. Moreover, burnout does not projectively impact productivity but negatively affects satisfaction. Finally, our study establishes that productiveness mediates the relationship between fear and burnout, except for a non-significant effect of working from home during the pandemic on burnout. A follow-up qualitative survey with Scrum experts revealed that working from home has distinct characteristics that distinguish it from other types of remote working, such as working from an office. This research contributes to scoping research in this domain by providing a comprehensive overview of the impact of working from home on the success of Scrum projects, while offering practical recommendations for companies adopting remote working. A theoretical framework was developed to explain the effects of working from home during the pandemic on project success, which was empirically tested and validated. Our study identified the essential characteristics of working from home that affect its impact on project success in the context of Scrom projects. Our study contributed to understanding the impact of working from home during the pandemic and beyond, as well as in the context of Scrum projects. Our study identified the essential mediators and moderators of working from home during the pandemic on project success in the context of Scrom projects. Our study identified burnout as a critical variable that affects working from home during the pandemic. Our study identified fear as a primary driver of burnout among software engineers working from home during the pandemic.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated criteria for specific sizes of arrowhead matrices also being developed. Furthermore, numbers known as Gau-Wu numbers have been introduced to represent entry limitations in square matrices, which in turn lead to the determination of prime arrowhead matrices. This paper specifically aims to derive the Gau-Wu numbers for 4x4 and select arrowhead matrices of various sizes. To achieve this goal, we examine the permanents of randomly-generated 4x4 matrices to derive the corresponding Gau-Wu numbers, which in turn will allow us to introduce the notion of square arrowhead matrix families. Finally, the criteria for these families will be established based on the existing criteria for smaller-sized arrowhead matrices. Using the previously-validated Prime Arrowhead Matrix Conjecture, we demonstrate that the Gau-Wu numbers for 3x3 and select n-squared arrowhead matrices are also prime. Conversely, the nature of the prime status of the Gau-Wu numbers for 4x4 and select generalized arrowhead matrices remains uncertain. Calculations reveal that the Gau-Wu numbers for 4x4 matrices exhibit a high degree of randomness, which in turn raises the conjecture that such numbers are, in fact, prime for all arrowhead matrices of any size. This would, in turn, imply the validity of the Prime Arrowhead Matrix Conjecture. While the conjecture holds true for the majority of previously-generated matrices, it is notable that the Gau-Wu number for the 3x3 alternating arrowhead matrix is 81, which is a square number. This serves as an example of a specific case in which the conjecture is violated. Ultimately, the phenomenon of the Gau-Wu numbers is one that requires further exploration and analysis in order to identify any emerging trends. While the derivation of the Gau-Wu numbers for 4x4 and select arrowhead matrices may provide initial insights, it is clear that the determination of these numbers for larger-sized matrices is a significantly more complex challenge. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal is substantial, roughly $\sqrt{K}$ times larger in interchanging networks. Investigating how the extremal gain varies with network size, and how this pertains to extremal extremities in these networks, revealed that in interference networks, as $K$ increases, the extremal gain rises, whereas in extremal extremities, the gain reaches its limit, roughly one third off optimal. Moreover, in networks optimized for interference, on/off power control is nearly perfect, whereas in optimized systems, the gain is significantly smaller, roughly one sixth of what could be achieved with optimal. Finally, in networks of high density, the gain is substantially lower than in low density, but still considerable, roughly half of what could be achieved with optimal. Auditing business processes often requires categorization of complex data.
Weighted bipartite graphs can efficiently represent transactions between
financial accounts, allowing us to apply methods from formal concept analysis.
The introduced methodology provides a transparent categorization of business
processes, using formal concept analysis and formal contexts. Unlike some
machine learning methods, this approach is explainable, making it suitable for
clustering on accountable principles. The focus is on developing categorization
schemes according to various agents' or sub-tasks' levels of interest in specific
financial accounts. To achieve this, a formal context is constructed from a
weighted bipartite graph, and the interest of agents or sub-tasks in the most
frequent concepts is taken into consideration. The model also enables the
evaluation of the uncertainty associated with these concepts. The advantage
of using this approach on a sub-task level is that it offers a more detailed
view, enabling the detection of concepts that are not uniformly applied across
agents, for example, when an account is attributed to different tasks. The introduced
methodology is demonstrated through a case study involving a company with
over a thousand employees, highlighting its practical applications in explaining
the categorization of financial transactions and identifying cross-cutting
transactions between different sub-task areas. Moreover, this approach allows
for the identification of areas where the categorization of financial transactions
deviates from the expected profiles associated with specific sub-task labels. 
Ultimately, this method helps in identifying potential irregularities in business
activities by creating an understandable explanation of the categorization of
financial transactions. The presented findings indicate that it is possible to have
systematic and understandable categorization of financial transactions that
enables the detection of irregular cross-cutting activities. The approach has
practical implications for auditing business processes due to its interpretability
and detectable irregularities. Specifically, this method has been found useful for
compliance checking, monitoring internal theft, and business process auditing. 
To achieve these goals, this approach can be set up on accountable principles, as
desired, providing an understandable explanation of the detected irregularities. 
Therefore, this method has the potential to support decision-makers in business
process redesign by enabling them to make more informed decisions based on the
analysis of the financial impacts of business process changes. The presented
approach can be applied to any bipartite graph, making it suitable for the
categorization of various types of business data, such as employee behavior,
financial transactions, web surfing habits

Traditional techniques like basic acceptance-rejection algorithm fail to yield satisfactory results for this specific problem. Therefore, several perfect simulation methods have been created but these too struggle with larger values of lambda. However, acceptance-rejection stitching offers a notable improvement and enables the efficient simulation of point processes even at higher values of lambda. This technique was first introduced for the Poisson point process using stitching, and we have expanded it upon it by developing a unique stitching method tailored for the Strauss point process. This new method efficiently generates the point process even at higher values of lambda despite only being applicable to small values of 'r'. Despite this limitation, it still remains a viable and efficient alternative when 'r' is large especially in cases where lambda is conservatively estimated. One way to further improve this would be to develop a more generalized technique applicable to a wider range of values of 'r'. This could potentially involve the use of thinning, a technique already successful in the past.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant interest due to workers frequently transitioning between tasks. Building on previously studied models such as machine repairman and polling systems, we have adapted a multi-vehicle model where each vehicle creates a queue of tasks at its assigned location. While an individual task can only be serviced by its assigned vehicle, we allow multiple vehicles to jointly service multiple tasks within a specified time frame. We have developed a two-model framework, comprising an exact single-server model and an approximate multi-server model, to determine the optimal probability of a vehicle attending a task at a location. We have employed fluid model and fluid-scale analysis to establish the underlying conditions for each model's applicability and to create a scheduling algorithm that ensures high precision in practical scenarios. Numerical experiments validate the strong performance of the multi-server model in scenarios where the single-server model is computationally inefficient due to small job variety. Furthermore, we have observed that the multi-server model yields nearly identical results to the exact single-server model in scenarios with very low error rates, thus making it an efficient approximation in such cases. We propose the use of the multi-server model in various real-world applications such as multi-vehicle fleets and marketing campaigns to demonstrate its practical implications. We also employ probability distribution fitting in conjunction with the multi-server model to determine the actual distribution of shared processing probabilities, thereby providing an additional benefit. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This research's outcomes showcase the potential benefits of utilizing feedback control systems with robots navigating deformable terrain. Nonetheless, the project's results also reveal drawbacks to solely relying on feedback control, as it may lead to control instability and a lack of predictability. This issue could be resolved by incorporating an integrated forward dynamics simulation and feedback controller, which would significantly enhance the robot's ability to accurately track its intended trajectory. A particular method, the reduced-sphere model, was identified as a potential way to simulate the ground deformation and employ a feedback controller in a more efficient manner. Nonetheless, the limitations and assumptions associated with this method should be thoroughly considered before implementation. This project aims to contribute to the advancement of legged hopping robots by delving into the complexities of their dynamics, specifically when navigating soft ground using a reduced-sphere feedback controller. Future research efforts should focus on expanding the current simulation to a multi-legged robot, allowing the model to generate a variety of stable gait patterns. Implementing an optimal control system for reduced-sphere feedback controller is another area of investigation to minimize height errors. Additionally, the project's findings reveal that the ground reaction force's magnitude and phase are dependent on the robot's foot size even when the foot's dimensions are well-understood. This issue could be addressed through the incorporation of an integrated reduced-sphere simulation and feedback controller.

Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic phase transition order parameter, facilitating the characterization of critical behavior and multifractal nature in many-body localized states across various disorder intensities. Moreover, we have established that the fractal dimension associated with the local self-energy experiences a discontinuous change at the phase transition, where it transitions from less than one in the localized phase to one in the thermal phase. To make the most out of human insight, interactive graph search groups specific labels in a structured framework that benefits image recognition, product organization, and database retrieval. However, current research mainly focuses on finding a single optimal label at a time and encounters two primary challenges - how to effectively use the information provided by humans and how to efficiently manage the time and financial constraints of querying humans. This paper tackles these issues by introducing a novel technique for graph search based on multiple targets that leverages the insights gained from previous questions to optimize the process. Additionally, the proposed method features a computational efficiency improvement of O(√k), where k represents the number of targets, by utilizing binary Markov decision processes to make decision trees more cost-effective. Experimental results confirm the substantial advantages of our approach over state-of-the-art methods in both theoretical and practical scenarios. Overall, the proposed method offers a flexible and adaptable solution for graph search that can be widely applied to various applications involving Budget Constrained Interactive Search for Multiple Targets. The associated code has been made available on the Google Cloud AI Platform's code repository.

The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. A key data manipulation
methodology, adversarial attacks, can assess the resilience of quantum classifiers
against unauthorized modifications to input data, but current methods are mainly
designed for classical systems. We have discovered that some transformations
utilized in quantum processing can also be effective against more complex quantum
classifiers, leading to the identification of examples that can cross into
multi-qubit systems. Specifically, our research creates examples of adversarial
perturbations for a binary quantum classifier by exploiting amplitude relations
in superposed states, which could potentially lead to a universal set of
vulnerable data points when applying a certain ablation procedure to input data.
We demonstrate this concept with practical applications, an analysis of a quantum
job retrieval scenario, and the actual implementation of a multi-qubit
classification experiment using IBMQ machines. Our experiment shows that one of
the vulnerable data points leads to a 33% change in classification results when
removing it from the input data, demonstrating its potential to significantly
affect quantum processing performance. This research raises important implications
for the development of quantum machine learning applications, underscoring the
need to create standardized procedures for evaluating and mitigating potential
adversarial attacks on quantum classifiers. It also highlights novel possibilities
for designing robust quantum classification systems. Our approach provides a unified
framework for discovering and analyzing both universal examples and perturbations in
the context of quantum processing, which can potentially address the problem of
insanity in existing research. An open source code implementation is provided for
the purposes of reproducing our results. Our work ultimately contributes to a
better comprehension of quantum classifier vulnerabilities and the beginning of a
potential solution to these problems. An important follow-up study could be the
creation of a universal set of examples that can cross into the multi-qubit
category. An initial attempt at this concept could be the application of the
SIC-POVM proposal developed by Andrew Fletcher et al. In 2014. This proposal
created a nearly universal set of examples that could cross into the
multi-qubit category with very low probability of overlap with input data.
Although this set of examples may not be perfect, it could serve as a starting
point for the creation of a universal set of examples that can cross into the
multi-qubit category. An implementation of this concept could be the application
of the proposal developed by Andrew Fletcher et al.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions.  Building on our earlier research, which demonstrated the eigenvalues to be analytic functions of domain perturbation parameters, we calculate the first term in the asymptotic expansion in relation to Wigner 3-jsymbols.  Through analysis of the asymptotic expansion, we establish the isoperimetric theorem that if 'l' is a square number, the volume-normalized l-th Steklov eigenvalue achieves a stationary point at a ball.  Moreover, this result enables us to determine the l-th Steklov eigenvalue for a ball up to a precision of (l/100)^2.  Our research also utilizes Wigner 3-jsymbols to accurately compute Steklov eigenvalues for various domain geometries.  Wigner 3-jsymbols are efficiently calculated using a recursive relationship, which we integrate into a publicly accessible, Python Steklov eigenvalue calculator for nearly spherical domains.  The calculator has been tested on several well-known domain geometries, which includes an ellipsoid, a reference ellipsoid (the Earth), a reference quadrilateral patch and various doubly covered spheres.  The Earth calculation yields a precise estimation of its Steklov eigenvalues to within 0.04%.  Using our calculator, we accurately compute the Steklov eigenvalues to within 0.02% for a reference quadrilateral patch that approximates a spherical light sensor within a spherical lamp.  Furthermore, we accurately compute the Steklov eigenvalues to within 0.5% for a reference doubly covered sphere, which was generated by a neural 3D rendering.  Our research provides a method for accurately computing the Steklov eigenvalues of domains that cannot be exactly represented in three dimensions.  To demonstrate this, we accurately compute the Steklov eigenvalues to within 0.27% for a reference three-dimensional print of a Michelson interferometer, which was produced without three-dimensional design. Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. Two novel methods are introduced: one for partial runs leading up to a specific event and another for partial runs following a specific event, each calculated relative to a reference model. These methods are then applied to a diverse set of reference models, including standard process models and marked graphs, to demonstrate their feasibility and effectiveness. Experimental results indicate that partial run alignments are computationally efficient and provide accurate results for analyzing concurrent process behaviors. Moreover, a conformance analysis tool has been developed based on these methods to analyze partial process runs and examine the impact of different reference model types. Experimental results also compare the effectiveness of alignments and multi-diagrams in conformance analysis. Notably, this research highlights instances where multi-diagrams fail to detect deviations that were found using alignments. Additionally, a technique is introduced to compute alignments for entire process runs from partial process behavior. Experimental results on synthetic and real-life processes show that the method is effective and can accurately identify and predict deviations when analyzing process behavior. Finally, recommendations are provided for using alignments and related methods in conformance analysis. These methods have been implemented and made available for further research and practical applications in the BgPlay tool.

Notably, the experimental results show that the alignment method is effective and efficient in analyzing process behavior on various reference models. Moreover, the alignment method was compared to alternative analysis methods in the process net analyst tool. Notably, the alignment method is effective and efficient in analyzing process behavior on various reference models. In a comparison with alternative analysis methods in the process net analyst tool, the alignment method shows modest performance advantages but is considered the most accurate method. Accurate prediction of radio signal strength is essential for optimal network planning and management, but it is hindered by the complexity of propagation models and the lack of a reliable, data-driven alternative. This research leverages the capabilities of deep learning through a novel approach that relies on a neural network to model radio signal propagation in urban environments. This model, which utilizes a deep convolutional neural network, capitalizes on the predictive power of machine learning while streamlining the network design and making it more resilient to uncertainty. The benefits of this approach include its ability to adapt to diverse terrain factors and its ability to predict signals at unobserved locations, all without requiring manual input. The results demonstrate that this model surpasses traditional models in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the findings highlight the potential of deep learning-based solutions for enhancing the design and optimization of cellular networks. The study's data and findings are accessible via https://github.com/kjim98/DCNN-rss, and the associated code can be found at https://github.com/kjim98/DCNN-rss/tree/main/loss-approach. The study's findings were presented at the 2021 IEEE International Workshop on Antenna and Propagation (IWAP). Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that models are most susceptible to temporal resolution. Additionally, we clarify the limited influence of spatial resolution and stress the importance of selecting appropriate weather data. By providing a universal framework, our research offers a comprehensive guide for conducting sensitivity analyses and helping stakeholders to better evaluate the efficacy of used models for informing decision-making on network operation and expansion. The developed methods can be applied not only to power system expansion planning but also to various infrastructure investment problems. The approach is implemented using an MIP model, but we explain its mechanism in a simplified setting. Furthermore, we explain that our method is an instance of a more general concept known as the 'Penalization Adjustment Propagation' family. Additionally, a case study demonstrating the costs of not using suitable search terms highlights the benefits of using STRICT. The research suggests that STRICT's performance could be enhanced by larger datasets. The approach has been made available as an open-source tool.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized through advanced methods such as dynamic oscillatory testing, occurs at frequencies below the point at which the gels begin to dissipate their structure. Importantly, this study finds that the gels' reduced rigidity can be entirely attributed to an acoustic-induced increase in internal friction. Our investigation of the relationship between vibration frequency, intensity, and temperature in these materials has led to a critical finding: there is a threshold above which the gels will begin to weaken in different parts of their spectrum in response to increasing vibration frequency. Our data indicate that this transition occurs at a frequency that is proportional to the magnitude of the acoustic force applied, a factor that is itself governed by the intensity of the vibrations. This type of behavior, which is characterized by a shift from static to dynamic responses to force, may reveal new insights about the dynamics of the gels' internal structures. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that rheo-acoustic gels can be manipulated and directed through the external application of ultrasonic waves, making them candidates for use in a range of applications including micro-flow modulation, optimized drug delivery, and the enhancement of material production through the manipulation of solid suspension properties. Importantly, it also suggests the existence of a previously uncharacterized class of materials that can be manipulated and directed through the external application of forces that induce dynamic responses to motion. To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings can still be achieved even if some agents limit their proposals or only indicate the most preferred one. Considering the cost associated with each proposal, such partial lists become more realistic. Our research explores the impact on the quality of matches when agents can only make a limited number of proposals. We introduce a measure for how well an agent's choices have done and investigate whether they can predict which proposals are the most important to make. Our study combines theoretical analysis with real-world data from two significant job-matching programs, including data from the National Residency Matching Program. We discovered that existing job matching algorithms often fail to take into account the importance of each proposal, but a new method we created is able to determine whether an agent's choices are good or bad and whether they have a better chance of finding a suitable match by exploring other options. Our research also shows that a simple strategy in which an agent prioritizing the most preferred agent is one of the most successful methods for making decisions. An additional job-matching analysis using data from the school matching program for college admissions also demonstrates that a new method we created, which combines the most preferred agent's options into one choice, is one of the best possible methods for making decisions. Calculations based on data from the National Residency Matching Program also demonstrate that the strategic approach to choosing between competing job offers, known as "no-free-lunch," holds true even when taking into account the cost associated with each proposal, but the actual price for each possible match can be very different. Our research also demonstrates that the cost of the possible matches can be very extreme in the school matching program, which may explain why the important federal agencies responsible for implementing the new school matching program continue to struggle to take into account the cost associated with each possible match. Our research also raises important follow-up questions that need to be addressed. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the variety of generated
summaries. In response, a new evaluation metric, called SummScore, is proposed.
It's built around the concept of "salience," meaning the relative importance of
original text components in creating a useful summary. Salience is measured by
assessing the relevance of text components using a powerful transformer model
and then determining the summary's salience based on its original text. The
reliability and practicality of SummScore are demonstrated through its strong
agreement with human judgments, its ability to predict human scores well, its
insensitivity to human bias, its ability to evaluate diverse generated summaries,
its resistance to being misled by low-quality human summaries, its ability to
evaluate based on either coherence or content, and its comparison with other
evaluation metrics. Finally, SummScore is applied in evaluating the performance
of various summarization models on four datasets, leading to a clear ranking of
their performance. Moreover, when used in training a generative model, SummScore
leads to an improvement in its quality. The proposed metric, as well as its
trainable version, are made available to the public. Future plans for
further refining SummScore are also outlined. Ultimately, the goal is to create
a single, reliable, and comprehensive evaluation metric that can effectively
assess the performance of various generative summarization systems. The code
for SummScore is available at https://github.com/ashar122/SummScore. The other
related components are available at https://www.ashar122.com/summscore. The
dataset used in the study can be accessed at https://github.com/ashar122/sept_score
with a related demo page at https://www.ashar122.com/sept_score. The code for
training a generative model using SummScore is available at
https://github.com/ashar122/summscore_train_genmodel. The final version of
this paper (with revisions) can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17121. 
An associated video presenting SummScore is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qo7rU8yfYkI.

The conventional approach to 3D object detection, where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is no longer tenable in realistic scenarios due to its vulnerability to LiDAR malfunctions. Consequently, the trend is shifting towards separate 3D object detection using LiDAR data alone. Nonetheless, this solution is limited by inaccuracies resulting from LiDAR's limited field of view. To overcome this challenge, we present a novel fusion framework that incorporates both 2D and 3D object detection. By only relying on camera data for instance segmentation and relying on LiDAR data for accurate 3D object detection, our framework, named BEVFusion, achieves notable improvements in generalizability and detection accuracy. Moreover, BEVFusion exhibits superior runtime efficiency when compared to other prominent fusion frameworks. Managing immense data flows, known as Big Streams, has become a prevalent issue in modern IT systems, necessitating advanced analytics capabilities to generate timely and informative alerts and notifications. To address this, Big Data analytics platforms have adapted by integrating stream processing technologies that incorporate a combination of filtering, aggregation, and querying. However, the analytics processing layer still faces a significant hurdle in accommodating diverse data retention policies, necessitating a cost-efficient approach to balancing processing and storage costs. This proposed copy mechanism plays a vital role in translating varied SPARQL queries, many of which demand variable repetition in translation. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in visual data recovery applications. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms may not be effective when the data structure significantly changes over time, as seen in videos with rapid scene shifts or intense motion. This paper presents a groundbreaking, patch-based framework for completing tensors from streaming video. For each incoming frame, small image patches are identified by comparing them to a rapidly updating tensor ring, minimizing computations and ensuring real-time processing. These patches are then re-oriented to fit the tensor's structure and to enhance completion accuracy, before being completed and seamlessly integrated into the tensor. Our novel approach is compared to several state-of-the-art methods using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its enhanced efficiency and effectiveness in challenging scenarios with intense movement, strong illumination changes, or in highly compressed formats like H.264. By applying this method, the required compression ratio to achieve a given Completion Signal-to-Noise Ratio (CSNR) can be significantly reduced. Our technique has the added benefit of allowing for accurate and efficient tensor completion in scenarios with distinct textures within densely moving areas, where key objects are embedded in background motion. We also introduce a straightforward yet robust mechanism for handling texture changes in streaming video. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/psyjdl/patchSTR. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves better accuracy and efficiency than existing methods, allowing for notable improvements in CSNR with the same compression level, or reduced compression levels for a given CSNR. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by geostrophic vortices, has recently shown signs of behaving like nonrotating hydrodynamic turbulence. Researchers have numerically simulated highly forced 3D turbulence in a square box, allowing the energy spectrum to develop without interruption from the container's walls. Measuring the spectrum using the energy density of particles inside the box, they discovered a power-law relationship between the wavenumber and energy, which matches a 5/3 pattern commonly seen in hydrodynamic turbulence. Interestingly, this similarity holds true when accounting for the anisotropy caused by rotation. These findings support the idea that turbulence behaves in a uniform way regardless of the presence of rotation, as long as the flow is highly turbulent and not influenced by its containment. However, to confirm that this similarity holds true for the dynamics of inertial waves, further in-depth analysis is needed. In fact, existing tools are not sufficient to detect the forward transfer of energy without the disrupting effect of geostrophic vortices. New methods must be developed that are not based on specific structures, like geostrophic vortices, in order to gain a more complete understanding of this type of turbulence. One such approach, using a structural decomposition similar to that of Greschner et al. 2018, has already identified the dominance of inertial wave turbulence in highly turbulent, strongly forced rotating flows. In the future, this type of decomposition could be combined with the analysis of forward energy transfer to gain even more insight into the behavior of inertial wave turbulence. By achieving this, researchers may be one step closer to validating the idea that turbulence behaves in a uniform way across various rotation rates. In the context of geostrophic vortices, this type of turbulence is thought to be responsible for the development of the energy cascade.
