Research demonstrates that indicator vectors representing maximal independent sets of the graph are the sole binary equilibrium states for IGN and they remain stable under specific parameter conditions. Furthermore, we show that these binary equilibrium states can either remain unchanged or diminish over time under certain graph conditions, and we provide an explanation for their eventual disappearance using the concept of a 'crown' consisting of a graph's maximum weight independent set, its neighbourhood and the edges connected to it. The study also provides an alternative understanding of the 'crown' using a particular metric called the Steinberg ratio, and it includes theoretical proofs to support the theoretical crowning process. In addition to the theoretical developments, the researchers also examined real-world graphs to observe the effects of IGN on their structural properties, and they have made the graphs used in the study available for public viewing. The researchers also explored the effectiveness of IGN in solving the Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem, and they have proposed a new approach for solving this problem based on their findings. The researchers tested various non-linear transformations and examined the influence of parameters on IGN's performance for different types of graphs. The study reveals that IGN is capable of identifying the exact solution for sparse graphs more quickly than existing methods, and it is highly robust, continuing to produce accurate results even under extreme circumstances. The researchers also discovered that IGN is highly resistant to attacks that aim to disrupt its performance and they provide evidence of this in the form of a contest where they challenged the research community to develop more advanced and efficient algorithms for solving MWIS by issuing a challenge on the Covert Nodes platform. The researchers also explored the effectiveness of IGN in compressing graphs while maintaining their structural properties, and they have proposed a new understanding of the 'crown' concept as a metric for measuring compression. Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emission from systems consisting of small cool stars called M dwarfs, which shares similar patterns to magnetospheric phenomena observed in our Solar System. The radio emission could be driven by a star-planet interaction or an unstable balance in a rotating disk and the surrounding stellar magnetic field. A new monitoring campaign observed the M dwarf system CR Draconis, consisting of multiple observing sessions taken over a period of approximately two years, which resulted in a substantial total on-source time of around six days. The study found that CR Draconis emits radio signals 90 percent of the time with low frequencies and has a specific polarised characteristic, as well as displaying circular polarisation and intense bursts. Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, whereas humans' learning of abstract patterns allows them to withstand extreme visual distortions. We propose a novel set of visual transformation methods rooted in neurophysiological research to evaluate the performance of both humans and networks on an object recognition task. We found that machines excel in certain transformations while faltering behind humans in simpler ones. We identified differences in human and machine accuracy using these transformations, ranked their effectiveness based on human results, and created the NeuroTest benchmark to assess the performance of both humans and networks using these challenging tasks. The full dataset, including data collected from both humans and networks, is available online at neurotest.org. Our research suggests that networks can learn more more efficiently if challenged with more demanding tasks, such as those used in the NeuroTest. By identifying and exploiting the strengths and weaknesses of both human vision and ANNs, we can develop a more efficient and innovative approach to designing more sophisticated computer vision systems. The NeuroTest's innovative approach provides valuable insights for machine learning designers to create more effective algorithms. Furthermore, our dataset can facilitate scientific studies on human vision, such as the cognitive processes involved in our proposed evaluation methods. We are providing the NeuroTest dataset free of charge to promote research in both computer vision and human vision to design more efficient neural networks. The dataset can be found at neurotest.org. The source code for implementing the NeuroTest and NetworkTransformer is also available online at neurotest.org. Our research and its related data and codes receive funding from the ERC, the NSF, the MPI for Biological Computing, and the Max Planck School for Computational Methods in the Life Sciences. The ERC supports as a top researcher the idea of bridging human and machine vision research. The NSF funds a collaborative research on bridging human and machine vision at UC Santa Barbara. The MPI for Biological Computing provides computational resources for the project and the dataset collection. The Max Planck School for Computational Methods in the Life Sciences promotes interdisciplinarity in data sharing to design more efficient neural networks. The dataset collection received additional funding from the MPI for Intelligent Systems and the University of Freiburg. The project was supervised by the Principal Investigator Dr. Konstantinos Demetressan and the co-advisors Dr. Felix Bernstein and Dr. Stephanos Roukas

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can specify a pre-existing prompt that induces the model to learn new classifications from text solely through self-supervised learning. However, identifying suitable prompts and training data remains an unsolved problem. To address this, researchers have proposed optimizing prompts and training data to enhance the model's zero-shot learning capabilities. To this end, a study presents a comprehensive dataset of prompts and training guidelines, collected from various sources, to facilitate the adaptation of pre-trained language models for zero-shot learning. Furthermore, a tool for analyzing and optimizing pre-trained language models on multiple prompts and datasets has been developed, allowing for the selection of the most effective configuration for a specific classification task. Through thorough evaluation, the meta-optimized GPT-3 model has demonstrated superior performance on multiple datasets and classification tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art results for zero-shot learning. Notably, the model achieved an accuracy of 66.8% on a dataset of code quotes with no training examples, successfully predicting the corresponding code snippet's author. You can access the source code and a user-friendly interface for zero-shot learning on GitHub. Research has shown that this interface can efficiently be applied to classify code snippets and sentences, as well as generate engaging stories. Furthermore, a study has been conducted to identify the most influential factors contributing to the model's accuracy on the CodeQuote dataset, revealing that specific word co-occurrences and length characteristics significantly impact performance. This study has majorly implications for multiple areas of study, as it reveals that a single multi-purpose language model can be applied to a variety of classification tasks. Additionally, a study has been conducted to investigate the possibility of utilizing pre-trained language models as general classifiers, as initially proposed by Peters et al., although they had initially considered this possibility only for binary classifications. Research has also been conducted to examine whether multi-shot learning, as opposed to zero-shot learning, could enhance the model's accuracy on the CodeQuote dataset. Results from this study indicate that, indeed, using a few examples during meta-tuning significantly improves the model's accuracy on the CodeQuote dataset. You can access additional studies on the GPT-3 model's capabilities and analyses in a companion paper, as part of a study on the recent breakthroughs and advancements in natural language processing. Research has also been conducted to conduct a thorough evaluation of the GPT-3 model's performance as a general classifier in a multi-shot setting.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, built upon vast language datasets. Nevertheless, these models are unresponsive to the underlying logical structure of the data, assuming a uniform distribution of outcomes. This limitation is prohibitive for critical applications, such as natural language interface, due to logic-based constraints. To address this, we introduce LogIT, an innovative parser that integrates a trusted logical input log that specifies permissible outcomes. The LogIT system incorporates a sequence alignment model, trained with augmented data from the logical input, yielding substantial enhancements in semantic parsing accuracy on various benchmarks, even when the logical input log comprises just a handful of ground truth sentences. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capacity of the sequence alignment model to identify incorrect sentences that aren't listed in the logical input log, indicating its potential to analyze logic-independent ambiguities. This research marks the first instance of a semantic parser achieving top-notch results on a diverse range of benchmarks, including TACCLUSTER, TACGB, ATIS, and SBU. Importantly, the LogIT system requires just a small amount of semi-supervised training data, making it well-suited for applications with limited resources. The code for the LogIT system is publicly available at https://github.com/jimmy1337/LogIT. The research is grounded on the developer-oriented semantic parser, DASP, first presented in IJCAI 2021. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation. Simulation experiments are also performed to assess the observer's performance in various epidemic scenarios. Furthermore, these conditions are illustrated through a concrete application of the observer design process for a nonlinear epidemic model that incorporates noise on the input channel. This model is motivated by the increasing importance of targeted intervention strategies due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Simulation results demonstrate the capacity of the observer design to handle such complex systems. This work aims to lay the groundwork for observing a broader class of nonlinear systems that exhibit state bifurcation and can be applied to various other epidemic models. Moreover, these conditions can be an essential tool for evaluating and interpreting the impact of nonlinear dynamics on error growth, particularly in systems with large norm large error growth that cannot be captured by linear designs. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this potential, existing static models have reached reasonably accurate results, even when compared to their temporal counterparts. Given the availability of techniques that enable the incorporation of time series properties, this paper aims to investigate the potential of static models by adapting them to generate more accurate predictions in temporal knowledge graphs. To this end, we employ a static model, called TPE, which has been developed for temporal knowledge graph applications, but now modify it to utilize static graph embeddings instead. Furthermore, we derive an optimized version of TPE, referred to as PTE, by replacing its conventional scoring function with a pairing-dependent one. We conduct experiments on multiple datasets, which demonstrate that both TAE and PTE outperform existing state-of-the-art models, including those that address temporal considerations. These findings suggest that static graph embeddings, when appropriately modified, possess the potential to significantly enhance performance in applications that involve temporal contexts. We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. These functions are linked to nested exponentials through a useful functional equation and have a series expansion that converges within a certain region of the complex plane. By examining the properties of $\beta$, we can study the dynamics of the exponential map $e^{\mu z}$ and obtain insights into the behavior of fractional iterations. Our analysis allows us to identify conditions under which Abel equations can be constructed from $\beta$ and to identify holomorphic functions of period $2\pi i / \lambda$ that serve as holomorphic Abel functions of the form $t(s+1) = e^{\mu t(s)}$. These functions play a key role in understanding iterated functions of the form $t(s+1) = \lambda t(s)+\beta$ and enable us to derive information about the iterated exponential function $t(s+1) = e^{\mu[s]}$. Our results are complemented by a proof that the function $e^{\mu s}$ is not holomorphic in the right half-plane for any value of $\mu$. This proof relies on a comparison with the function $\beta_{0, \mu} (s)$ and highlights a key difference between the two functions within the region where their series expansions converge. Finally, we have established a connection between the function $\beta$ and Kneser's natural tetration. Our analysis shows that the natural tetration can be constructed from $\beta$ under a certain condition that involves the hyperplane $s = 0$. Outside of this context, however, we have found that the function $\beta$ is not sufficient to construct the natural tetration since its Abel equation cannot be holomorphically extended to the left of this hyperplane. These findings provide insight into why Kneser's tetration cannot be constructed from iterated exponentials. They also provide insight into the reason for the breakdown of holomorphic continuity in the complex plane, which is evident in plots of $\beta$ and related functions. In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform. Our results demonstrate that modeling user intent using our approach yields better user experiences and higher overall satisfaction. Moreover, our approach enables the discovery of rich, abstract user preferences that are difficult to detect in user behavior data alone. These preferences can be leveraged by the platform to create a more personalized experience for users and enhance their long-term value to the platform. We've discussed the broader platform benefits of our approach in section 7.2. Lastly, we've highlighted several potential areas of improvement for future research and development.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These findings are based on an innovative model transformation from the homogeneous to a heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model. We demonstrate that some PCA-based methods are optimal in certain scenarios but suboptimal in others. Numerical experiments comparing these findings with PCA-based methods and other optimization techniques such as gradient descent and message passing are also provided. We further demonstrate that a simple PCA-based technique can be the optimal method for distinguishing signal and noise in certain cases, but not in cases where noise dimensions are large compared to the number of matrix ranks. Additional numerical experiments comparing these methods are provided. This research is the first to establish recovery boundaries in an infinite-dimensional setting for a wide range of low-rank matrix estimation problems. It is based on novel mathematical insights, including the development of a new low-rank matrix tensor product model, and mathematical techniques to derive precise statistical inference in this model. We demonstrate that some PCA-based methods perform well in cases where noise dimensions are small, and a simple change of variables reveals how these methods perform poorly in cases where noise dimensions are large. We also identify additional opportunities for improving low-rank matrix estimation methods using this new tensor product model and mathematical insights. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states. Lastly, a class of exceptional modes is proposed, where an exceptional point manifests as a universal property of the system, unaffected by either symmetry or any underlying structure. This new class of EM offers fresh insights into the relationship between symmetry and topology in bulk and boundary states. Our work introduces a novel topological model in the absence of symmetry, characterized by fractional boundary states and exceptional modes, and provides a groundbreaking understanding of the relationship between symmetry and topology in bulk and boundary states. It also opens doors for exploring various types of symmetry-breaking phase transitions at both bulk and boundary levels. Additionally, this work lays the groundwork for further investigations into the fractional phases that arise when symmetry is broken. We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained on randomly sampled CT volumes, and subsequent steps utilize the network to extract embedding features from the full scan volume. Averaging these features by segments, a second BERT model aggregates the multiple segments into a unified feature for final classification. By combining both classification stages, we achieve a high validation accuracy of 0.9164 in macro F1 score. Moreover, our approach effectively handles data scarcity issues by utilizing the initial model to extract features on the training dataset and then transferring these features to new, unrelated datasets for classification. Finally, our framework demonstrates the capacity to produce reliable diagnostics on limited data sets and underscoring the need for more efficient data sharing between hospitals to enhance pandemic response. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales.  We expand the scope of eco-evolutionary dynamics by exploring the interplay between different rates of change: slow, fast, and intermediate.  We show how modifying rate scales can transform unexpected outcomes from eco-evolutionary theory into new predictions.  For instance, using modified rates, we can explain how low genetic diversity can persist without collapsing into local extinctions. We achieve these outcomes through a phenomenological approach, effectively rewriting equations to account for different rates of change.  We then apply these modified models to hypothetical scenarios, including the dynamics of decaying species and conflicting evolutionary pressures that prey on a single host.  Our results demonstrate that adjusting the rate scales of eco-evolutionary models can yield diverse and rich outcomes, encompassing various levels of change over various periods.  We conclude by acknowledging the need for more research on long-term and intermediate timescales, similar to the focus on rapid changes, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay between ecology and evolution.  We also introduce modulators that can control and switch rates, enabling the application of eco-evolutionary theory to problems not originally considered within its scope, including climate change, biodiversity, and evolution.  For instance, we apply the theory to predict how conflicting environmental changes might contradict typical evolutionary trade-offs, leading to unexpected outcomes.  We also identify potential applications of eco-evolutionary theory to the understanding of long-term and intermediate timescales and suggest areas for future research.  Overall, our approach seeks to integrate fast, slow, and intermediate timescales into a unified theory of eco-evolutionary dynamics, expanding the scope of eco-evolutionary theory and its potential applications in real-world settings.  We provide supporting code on a GitHub page and include additional files describing our phenomenological approach and its application to the identified problems. A new analytical approach, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, focuses on the reliable inference of an outcome's value based on an ordinal test, particularly when only the rank of the test results is known. We developed this analysis to address the challenge of making inferences about an HIV trial, where participants were tested for their CD4+ lymphocyte count using an ordinal scale. Due to the absence of data on HIV's progression, we rely solely on the rank of the test results. We define a measure of uncertainty, referred to as the E-value, which serves as a key indicator for making reliable inferences. Through simulation, the E-value is shown to effectively distinguish between the reliable and unreliable inferences. We conduct an extensive analysis of the HIV trial data, combining the E-values from individual and pooled analyses to make more precise inferences about the trial's outcome. Our results reveal important implications for statistical analysis, particularly when data are divided into groups, as the choice of methodology greatly affects the accuracy of the inferences. Therefore, researchers must carefully consider the methodology to make reliable conclusions. Our approach is presented through an easily implemented R package, referred to as the Evalue package. Due to the absence of data on cannabis' effects, we rely solely on the rank of the test results. Using the E-value, we make informed inferences about its potential to impair memory. Our results underscore the significance of conducting sensitivity analyses when drawing conclusions from experimental data. Additionally, the E-value has potential as a versatile metric for statistical analysis, potentially expanding into related fields such as computational biology and machine learning. This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, incorporating both local and general voting processes. Specifically, a comprehensive evaluation of various source selection algorithms in conjunction with different voting mechanisms reveals the importance of balancing the global vision with more focused, detailed observations. Furthermore, this technique is exemplified through its application in facilitating navigation for autonomous robotics. Subsequently, a large-scale experiment is demonstrated, showcasing the technique's capabilities by generating three-dimensional points of interest within a 16 square kilometer area of a bustling city, encompassing over 350 million considerations. Consequently, empirical analysis of this data reveals a substantial, nearly 20-fold increase in localization precision when leveraging this voting-based method as opposed to conventional approaches utilizing single image-based estimates. In addition to mathematical formulations describing the proposed algorithm, the accompanying code has been publicly released for reference at: https://github.com/AutonomyLabs/VALUE. Future research objectives are outlined, including the extension of this technique to account for dynamic objects within urban environments. Ultimately, future developments aim to establish a comprehensive, high-level dataset representing the spatial structure of a city, analogous to the successful 'ImagNet' concept within the computer vision community. This ambitious goal, dubbed 'UrbanImagelab', aims to establish a pioneering approach for autonomous navigation and decision-making in complex metropolitan settings. A preliminary exploration demonstrating the feasibility and benefits of this concept is presented, highlighting its potential to stream various 2D maps directly onto an autonomous system, thereby facilitating seamless decision-making. A particularly noteworthy application arises in cases where a 'blind' autonomous system is introduced to a unfamiliar environment, exemplified by a RL agent entering a unfamiliar video game world. Although this idea remains largely theoretical at the present time, our prediction is that a scalable and efficient solution will likely emerge in the not-so-distant future. Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy proves particularly effective in multiple error scenarios, particularly where the noise factor and the gate's inverse have distinct physical implications. We successfully integrated this noise-mitigation approach within a variational quantum eigensolver running on a superconducting quantum processor to find the ground-state energy of the hydrogen molecule, and observed substantial energy fluctuations reductions during the parameter learning process in the VQE algorithm. This advancement resulted in the reduction of necessary iterations to reach a stable value. In addition to hardware experimentation, our findings include comprehensive numerical simulations examining the influence of various noise models, randomized compilation, and the interplay of these components on the complex loss landscape of the problem at hand. These investigations have helped to clarify that the utility of this noise-mitigation approach depends on the specific characteristics of the errors affecting the quantum hardware. When errors are recurrent and the randomized compilation technique is employed, we have shown that the hidden inverse noise-mitigation strategy may not provide any direct benefit to the stability of the quantum algorithm. Instead, it might actually make the loss function more sensitive to varying gate timings, which can exacerbate learning difficulties during the parameter evolution in the VQE algorithm. This behavior can be attributed to the occurrence of partial entanglement wobbling, a phenomenon similar to experimentally observed phenomena where the loss function exhibits multiple local optima due to system instability. Ultimately, our research has highlighted that the application of the hidden inverse noise-mitigation approach to a quantum phase estimation algorithm may not always yield the anticipated outcome of reduced coherent errors, but rather depends on the specific characteristics of the quantum device in use. The detailed analysis presented in our study provides valuable insights for effectively integrating this noise-mitigation strategy in quantum computing applications. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this study reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNN), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, DCNN systems often rely on fixed, pre-defined orientation normalization approaches, such as data augmentation or image transformation within the network, which can be imperfect and introduce additional parameters that increase computational burden. In response, we propose a novel model, the Orientation Convolutional Network (O-Net), which leverages specific neural architecture designs to tolerate orientation transformations without the need for explicit transformation normalization. O-Net achieves this by including a specialized pathway that allows the network to learn orientation-invariant representations through a self-learning process. By removing the need for pre-defined transformation normalization methods, O-Net significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models on multiple image recognition tasks, including zero-shot and few-shot learning applications. Notably, O-Net can also be applied to tasks involving more severe domain shifts, such as multi-modal and large-domain vision recognition tasks. Furthermore, our model can be easily extended to support multiple orientation shifts. Through thorough experimentation, we validate the effectiveness of O-Net and provide insight into its internal learning mechanisms. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the theoretical representation learning behaviors of O-Net, demonstrating that the network's distinct architecture leads to the formation of an intrinsic transformation-sensitive channel that tolerates orientation transformations. Our findings are expected to facilitate the development of more robust image recognition systems for tasks involving significant domain changes. To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integration of mesh generation methods. The proposal splits the process into two stages: In the initial phase, we develop a high-order mesh on a coarsely tiled surface, utilizing a topologically ordered structure. To achieve this, we apply constraint programming to optimize mesh topology at a coarse level, ensuring a high-order layout with minimal errors. In the subsequent phase, we refine the mesh using advanced refinement methods, maintaining the high-order layout initially defined. Unlike other high-order mesh generation methods, our approach enables efficient domain subdivision with robust and high-order points, thus producing meshes of high quality, particularly on complex CAD models. We describe the method details and showcase several examples of high-order meshes on complex CAD models. The meshes can be used for high-order finite element analysis, multigrid-based computations, or high-speed mesh refinement in low-order finite element analysis. The method details and example meshes are publicly available at https://github.com/mr-ziyuanli/HighOrderQuadMeshGeneration. The meshes were implemented using the Gmsh mesh generator, the Coqmesh mesh generator, and the PyCoQmesh Python interface, which are all open-source tools. The meshes were generated using the superglue mesh generation strategy, the collapsing set strategy, the collapsing simplified strategy, the superset strategy, the superrefined set strategy, the infine set strategy, and the infine refined set strategy SUPGGE-CAS2. Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by providing 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries have limitations, such as 
restricted accessibility and limited word definitions. A potential solution is 
an online dictionary that stores extensive, freely updatable word definitions. 
However, current online dictionaries like Wiktionary and Wordnik have shortcomings 
in the form of insufficient definitions for some words and non-uniform 
accessibilities across different languages. To address these issues, we have created 
the Mind Dictionary, a centralized online dictionary providing comprehensive word 
definitions across multiple languages and symmetrical hyperlinks for efficient 
reference. Additionally, the Mind Dictionary is designed with an open-source 
architecture to enable seamless updates and the incorporation of user-generated 
content. The Mind Dictionary can serve as a model or inspiration for similar 
projects, while our accompanying paper outlines the intricacies of creating and 
maintaining such a dictionary.

Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for complex models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have demonstrated that an enhanced LIME explanation method, LIME-RS, for ranking systems not only enhances user satisfaction but also fosters increased user trust. However, the underlying factors that motivate users to rely on these explanations are still unclear. This study provides a new set of four criteria to evaluate the quality of these explanations: the explanation's coherence, its consistency with the model's behavior, its ease of comprehension, and its consistency over multiple model runs. The researchers utilized these criteria to refine the construction of LIME-RS explanations and showed that utilizing all four criteria leads to improved user satisfaction and increased confidence in the model's performance in a real-world ranking system. The findings from this study reveal the significance of both the explanatory method's design and the environment in shaping user perceptions of the quality of these explanations. Additionally, the researchers discovered that an optimal density level for LIME-RS explanations exists and that it may not always align with expectations. This study provides a new set of criteria for the evaluation of Explainable AI (XAI) explanations and offers a method for refining the design of LIME-RS explanations, ultimately improving their performance in real-world scenarios. The researchers conducted a series of experiments using a popular movie recommendation system and found that an LIME-RS density of 0.75 yielded the most favorable user responses. Notably, the study found that an LIME-RS density of 0.25, although expected, actually led to decreased user satisfaction. Possible reasons for this outcome are discussed, and the study recommends the use of explainability metrics that account for both the coherence and consistency of LIME-RS explanations to enhance our understanding of the LIME method in the context of ranking systems. Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an extraordinary chance to study these impacts in a star system. Our study involves over two years of space-based UV observations of AU Mic spanning multiple flare events, during which we detected two strong flares on AU Mic in the FUV range. Utilizing UV data for five quiescent and two flare episodes, we gathered spectra for three spectral lines: the P~11 line at 121.78 nm, the P~22 line at 273.14 nm, and the Lyman-α line at 121.54 nm. Our analysis measures a mean flux of 4.0 × 10^−2 photon cm^−2 s^−1 for the P~11 line, 2.0 × 10^−2 s^−2 photon cm^−2, and 2.0 × 10^4 photon cm^−2 s^−1 for Lyman-α. Furthermore, we find that the UV spectrum of AU Mic exhibits two distinct components, comprising a hot (T~10^4 K) component dominating its continuum and a cooler (T~10^3 K) component dominating its line emission. In the context of its planets, we find that the combined effects of radiation pressure and stellar particle emission could potentially eject planets inside the circumstellar disk around which AU Mic is located. Our research suggests that AU Mic's UV radiation originates from two distinct sources, one within its chromosphere and another within its disk photosphere. With an estimated mass flow of 1.0 × 10^(-8) M_earth/yr for AU Mic b and 1.0 × 10^(-7) M_earth/yr for AU Mic c, it's believed that these planets may remain intact for a substantial portion of their lifetimes, specifically 1.0 × 10^7 and 2.0 × 10^7 years for AU Mic b and c respectively, before they're lost due to their low masses. Our research also reveals that the UV-bright AU Mic could potentially harbor a highly active planet, which if existing, would have a minimum mass of 5.0 M_earth. Our research highlights the significance of monitoring active stars to determine the long-term impacts of their activities, especially in the context of their planetary systems

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Larmor formula accurately describes the energy lost due to radiation. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as robustness to outliers and resistance to shifting values. This method has been successfully tested on the WSJ Corpus, and the results show that it equals or surpasses state-of-the-art duration modelling in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, we examine the performance of a synthesis system that trains the duration model with a mixed training objective and compare it to a conventional method. The findings indicate that the proposed approach results in slight improvements in generalization, while also reducing training time. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that the proposed median-based strategy leads to significant improvements in duration modelling. An on-demand audio material is available at https://dx.com/median-durations. 

Medians are known to be robust to outliers, which makes them ideal for modelling the transition probabilities. One of the key benefits of median-based generation is the ability to produce synthesis data that is less likely to include extreme values. This can be particularly valuable in applications where the synthesis data needs to closely resemble the test conditions, such as when the training and test data have different characteristics, or if the model itself introduces irregular values due to its stochastic nature. 

In addition to the success of median-based generation, the proposed approach also equals or improves upon state-of-the-art duration modelling methods. Specifically, when compared to a conventional HMM-based method and a more recent transformer-based method, the proposed approach showed significant results. Importantly, the proposed approach does not rely on specific distribution types or mean durations for synthesis, which makes it a more general solution.

Finally, the proposed approach demonstrates the value of a objective-only training protocol, which can reduce training time by more than 50% compared to the standard 100% data approach. Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content, respectively. This research assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on deep neural networks and those that leverage word embeddings, such as Word2Vec and GloVe. Our findings also explored the efficiency of models that extract key features compared to those that rely on full texts. Our results demonstrate that models that utilize deep learning and professionally annotated data achieve better results, and that manually curated feature sets can be an acceptable alternative when annotated data is limited. Notably, our team established new benchmarks for subtasks one and two, and we explored various feature sets to identify the most effective for each task. A complementary publication has also discussed the impact of hyperparameter tuning on the model's performance. Both studies used the same data and experimental settings, but focused on the optimization process. A comparison of our work with existing studies reveals that our model's performance surpasses existing results for subtasks one and two, and we also investigated the potential for using transfer learning as an additional method to improve model performance. This study is available on arXiv, and our code is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/tony6017/Hate-Speech-ID.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that accurately describes a flexible robotic joint as a two-mass system with pose-dependent inertia, nonlinear friction, nonlinear elasticity, and backlash. A feed-forward controller is designed using the flatness-based method to optimize movement quality, and a supplementary feedback controller is implemented to counteract external disturbances, utilizing real-time automatic differentiation to enable rapid processing. Finally, the proposed algorithms are tested in simulated and real-world experiments using a KUKA Quantec KR300 Ultra SE. Experimental results indicate that the proposed methods significantly enhance position accuracy by reducing systematic positional errors resulting from backlash, and also demonstrate resistance to external disturbances by protecting the desired movement trajectory. This results in, for instance, a mere 0.015 mm positional deviation when lifting a load of 20 kg at 0.5 rad/s, and also shows that the position error due to backlash when moving under a load at 0.5 rad/s is minimized from 4.2 to 0.6 mm. This technology has potential for application in various machining processes such as milling, grinding, and other precision-based operations. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Inspired by the examination of social life patterns, which involve analyzing changes in various aspects of a person's social life, a new research method is proposed that utilizes multiple time-related health data to create classifications of different social life patterns. By incorporating both environmental and lifestyle factors, this approach aims to generate classifications that represent distinct life trajectories. When applied to a study on how people with heart attacks lead their lives, this new method demonstrated that factors such as physical activity and smoking are connected to the length of time a person remains free from other serious health issues. Additionally, the research found that people who had a heart attack were more likely to exhibit certain behaviors before the incident and that these behaviors were often influenced by psychological factors as well as environmental and lifestyle factors. The proposed methodology is called multiple state analysis, and it was utilized for conducting in-depth studies on multiple aspects of a person's life. It also led to the development of a computer-based tool, called lifeCourse, which enables researchers to create their own classifications based on multiple time-related health data, and it was applied in a study on how people with heart attacks lead their lives. Results from this study revealed that people who had a heart attack were more likely to exhibit stressful behaviors such as overeating, lack of physical exercise, and smoking, and they were also more likely to die from other serious health issues. However, the research found that people who remained healthy throughout their lives were more likely to engage in positive behaviors such as eating healthy food, staying physically active, and not smoking. It was observed that environmental and lifestyle factors are often interconnected and influence future health paths. And finally, the research was conducted on a study of how people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) lead their lives, and it was discovered that people who remained healthy throughout their lives were more likely to engage in positive behaviors such as staying physically active and avoiding smoking. It was also observed that environmental and lifestyle factors are often interconnected and influence future health paths. One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits slow convergence when applied to free electronic states found in processes like photoionization, this modified version achieves efficient results comparable to those for bound states. To accomplish this, the modified scheme incorporates a unique transition mechanism where atomic weights are gradually deactivated at a distance of a few bond lengths from their respective atomic nuclei and replaced by a smoothly converging weight that tends toward unity. Following this method, the integrals associated with atomic sites are calculated using smaller spherical grids, while the interstitial regions' residual integrals are calculated with a central grid. This method's accuracy has been demonstrated in various scenarios involving complex Gaussian, Yukawa potentials, and spherical Bessel functions, which reflect the nature of integrands found in realistic simulations of molecular scattering and photoionization. For reference, the source code for this scheme, in terms of the Fortran programming language, is provided as supplementary material. Furthermore, the modified scheme offers an appealing solution to implement sparse algorithms for systems featuring rotational symmetry, as illustrated in an example that involves the single center quadrature scheme. In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster. Moreover, we found the problem to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the distance to clique parameter. Due to the problem's complexity under the vertex cover number remaining unclear, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by the vertex cover number in constrained graph classes such as chordal, semiherditable, Ptolemaic, and split. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  An algebraic structure is also introduced for these spaces and shown to have a natural interpretation as lattices with Scott topology's lower/upper/adjointly-complete subspaces.  This work is further extended to the dual case of spaces with inverse directions.  Along with this, a new algebraic model for directed spaces and partial orders with Scott topology is introduced and proven to be equivalent to the categorical model.  The existence of partial orders with certain topological properties (for example, Scott open and Scott-closed spaces) is shown and shown to have a 1-1 correspondence with their powerspace algebras.  The paper concludes with further extensions and comparisons to other related work.  This research was supported by the National Research Foundation (NRF) of South Africa. Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior climate modeling has failed to resolve turbulent air motions and cloud dynamics directly, leaving significant gaps in understanding hothouse climate processes. In this research, simulations resolving convection explicitly found that 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating shifts the water cycle from steady state to a periodic regime, characterized by intense precipitation and long dry spells. The transition to this regime was associated with increased local precipitation and cloud cover, along with a positive climate feedback that may stabilize 'hothouse' environments. The research implies the presence of a new type of temporal atmospheric self-organization, affecting both cloud formations and erosion in hothouse climates. The potential implications of these findings are significant for the development of cloud-parameter schemes in climate models. We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, an expansion of Yang-Mills theory itself. This theory's twistor action builds directly upon Yang-Mills theory's original form. Consequently, this discovery yields further validation for the theoretical links between Yang-Mills theory and twistor theory, as well as the emergence of Yang-Mills theory from first principles. Moreover, this theory offers a preliminary prototype for studying higher-spin theories via a twistor-based framework. Theoretical implications and applications of this discovery remain an ongoing area of investigation. Theoretical implications and applications of this discovery are still being explored.

To address this issue, we developed a technique that utilizes Bayesian statistics to select and improve (refurbish) unreliable labels, thereby enhancing the quality of training data. By combining a conventional deep neural network with a Bayesian posterior probability distribution, we constructed a novel learning mechanism that effectively detects and rectifies individual label errors. Additionally, our method allows for the overall accuracy of the training data to be significantly improved, as reflected by the results from two benchmark datasets, specifically Imageset1 and Imageset2, which encompass a total of eight noisy medical image classification tasks. As compared to existing techniques, our proposed approach achieves greater robustness and reliability in the face of varying levels of noise intensity. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive empirical analysis to demonstrate the efficacy of our method, thereby validating its practical applications in quality-enhancing medical image labels for the purpose of classification. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist that are less intrusive than traditional approaches. We present a new theory of advanced integers that serves as the foundation of this alternative approach. By utilizing a dependent type for recursion, we are able to define non-terminating functions in a more natural and concise manner. We demonstrate the practical applicability of this method in a proof assistant setting, specifically in the context of HOL Light proofs. Further, our approach allows for the flexible integration of a clock as desired, rather than being enforced globally. Ultimately, we evaluate the benefits and trade-offs of our method in comparison to more conventional techniques. We contend that our approach represents an improvement in terms of elegance, and that the key to this improvement lies in understanding the mathematical structure of advanced integers. While our foundation may be more abstract than certain conventional clocks found in theoretical work, we believe it offers a useful insight. Conversely, we note that our approach does not simplify the problem of proving the equivalence of two functions, a common challenge in HOL proofs. In order to solve this problem, we recommend utilizing a counterexample-based strategy using the theorem prover HOL Light. We acknowledge that our approach may not be suitable for certain low-level, bit-level reasoning tasks commonly associated with theoretical work within HOL. However, for high-level theoretical work in a proof assistant setting, we argue that our method provides useful insights and potentially serves as a bridge to more abstract mathematical concepts. Ultimately, we hope this work may serve as a useful introduction to the theory of advanced integers, providing a deeper understanding of the mathematical foundation. Similar concepts have previously been applied in the context of functional programming by concrete type specialisation, we explore their potential generalisation within a logical framework. This study aims to establish a new approach for identifying the 3-D geometric characteristics of significant, swirling motions within wall turbulence, allowing these to be directly integrated into existing models for predicting wall-bound flows. This approach is data-driven, supported by large-scale numerical simulations of wall-bound flows and statistical testing, revealing a distinct link between the prevalence of these swirling structures and the level of turbulence intensity within the flow. However, the investigation also uncovers some limitations and potential sources of difficulty in implementing this approach in experiments due to the significant variability in the prevalence of these swirling structures at different turbulence intensities, particularly at lower levels. Furthermore, in cases where these swirling structures are less prevalent, reliance on examining the characteristics of individual instances of them proves insufficient for accurately capturing their geometric characteristics. In contrast, a more comprehensive statistical examination of the nonlinear co-occurrence of these swirling structures within the flow, rather than individually, yields a more consistent understanding of their characteristics. As an example of this new approach, existing models for predicting wall-bound flows, incorporating the geometric characteristics of these swirling structures, have been refined using data from large-scale numerical simulations. Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Nucleation of defects, scars and folds in curved crystals, as well as rearrangements of cells in biological tissue, all exhibit this phenomenon.  A theoretical framework, proposed by Martin and others, models mechanical screening through the accumulation of localized defects, effectively creating an 'electrical double layer' that facilitates and maintains screening.  We have conducted experiments and numerical simulations on discrete mechanical systems, specifically one-dimensional and two-dimensional bond-damper-element networks that mimic and mimic mechanical properties, and obtained results supporting the 'anomalous screening' theory.  A novel method for detecting and analyzing the emergence of geometric defects, rather than simply deformations, has been developed, and employed to study mechanical screening in granular columns and chains.  We demonstrate that geometric defects, (i) their formation (ii) their size distribution (iii) their mobility (iv) their correlation with stress fluctuations are all influenced by the screening process, (v) confirming that the 'anomalous screening' theory is applicable to these granular columns and chains.  Furthermore, our findings reveal that the time scale of the geometric defects' emergence, their peak density, and the time over which the systems are subjected to stress, are crucial parameters that govern the system's mechanical properties, and can be utilized to optimize mechanical performance, and that the 'anomalous screening' theory is a universal phenomenon that can be observed in a diverse range of discrete mechanical systems.  These conclusions are supported by numerical simulations and experimental results, and our methodology provides a template for investigating and quantifying mechanical screening in a wide scope of materials and systems.  Ultimately, our study reveals that the 'anomalous screening' theory is a dominant phenomenon that can be observed in a diverse range of discrete mechanical systems. This study analyzes data from the U.S. to determine how local newspapers cover the coronavirus and how their coverage correlates with infection rates. An examination of 327 daily newspapers and corresponding COVID-19 data from 28 states over a 12-month period found significant positive relationships between coverage and cases/deaths in the first 6 months, but only with cases in the second 6 months. Local newspapers in areas with higher percentages of lower-income and minority populations reported lower COVID-related headlines. An event study revealed an initial surge in coverage across the board, but it was short-lived for small and low-income area newspapers. Moreover, newspapers serving primarily low-income and minority populations covered the pandemic less extensively. Data from Facebook indicate that local newspapers with smaller audiences, particularly those having less extensive coverage of COVID-19 related topics, tended to have fewer readers who followed related topics. In summary, local newspapers' COVID-19 coverage in the U.S. varied based on the size and income of the area they served. While most newspapers covered the pandemic in its early stages, those serving large cities and high-income areas underreported it, according to COVID-19 data. Notably, a similar pattern was observed in Facebook data, where local newspapers with smaller audiences, primarily those serving large cities and high-income groups, underreported the pandemic. Ultimately, the findings suggest that local newspapers need to boost their coverage, particularly of underrepresented groups, to effectively address the coronavirus and other critical issues. Additionally, the study highlights the advantages of using Facebook's Audience Research Tool in news research. An associated website enables users to access and analyze the data collected in this research.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain unaltered when supplemented with a fast multipole method. This is conditioned on the correct application of Wigner D-matrices and point matching operators. This insight holds for both scalar and vector fields. A detailed proof has been given for conservative FMM schemes in both near and far field contexts for scalar case. Additionally, the mathematical underpinnings of conservative FMM have been applied to achieve a stable and efficient scalar potential method. This has an important application in computational studies of rigid body dynamics interacting with fluid scalar fields. The implementation of conservative angular momentum evolution for near field interactions alongside conservative far field interactions results in both computational and practical efficiencies, specifically in terms of reducing coupling matrix calculations by a factor of 9. This combination of methods is known as the Hybrid Particle-Grid Approach. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a foundation for examining and evaluating different interaction schemes, particularly in terms of near field coupling, which at present involves the standard SPH-D differentiation matrix operator. This could potentially be replaced with alternative methods, such as meshless Dirichlet-Neumann interactions or novel approaches that optimize coupling matrices for improved efficiency. Further research is necessary to identify these potential alternatives and evaluate their performance relative to the existing framework. This paper demonstrates the feasibility of achieving conservative efficient interactions, which serves as a stepping stone for developing novel interaction schemes in the future. To verify the proposed framework several test cases were employed including rotation, fluid-float simulations and the impact of a solid object into a stationary fluid. Results from these test cases not only confirm the conservation of angular momentum but also highlight potential issues with meshless interactions, which can result in unstable or poorly damped dynamics that could potentially be rectified with the implementation of novel interaction schemes. Furthermore, the proposed framework has significant implications in terms of optimizing interaction methods, which will be explored in depth in upcoming research. The relevant test cases were implemented in the Chombo-SPH code, a hybrid framework combining conservative particle methods with conservative grid-based methods. This code is unique in nature, bringing together conservative particle and grid interactions for efficient computational simulations. This paper documents the proposed framework and its implications, which has significant potential in terms of achieving efficient computational methods for interacting multi-body dynamics. Following this work, further research will be explored in a companion paper, where conservative interactions for high-order materials will be presented. This will not only expand the theoretical framework but also have far-reaching implications in terms of achieving efficient computational methods for a wide array of application domains

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it leverages the expertise of a guiding model to shape a student model's behavior. In order to accomplish this, we implement our proposed method, augmented policy cloning, which introduces artificially generated states to a training environment, making the system sensitive to its surroundings, thus greatly reducing the need for direct interaction with the environment for the learning model to perfectly replicate its mentor's actions. We achieve highly efficient behavior transfer from experienced to novice models, especially for tasks that require precise control. We test the efficiency of our proposed method by comparing its effectiveness to existing learning techniques and demonstrate its practical value in real-world scenarios involving two key settings: (1) reducing a student model's computational load by minimizing its parameter count, and (2) enabling knowledge transfer from experienced models with a unique understanding of their environment, possibly due to access to privileged information. In both cases, our proposed method continuously generates a flow of adjusted parameters in real-time, allowing novice models to adapt their behavior according to specific requirements. We validate the feasibility of our proposed method by successfully implementing it on both a challenging, high-stakes environment (urban driving) and a sensitive, high-stakes setting (microsurgical procedures). We conduct thorough experimentation to ensure our proposed method consistently yields compact yet accurate student models with predictable error margins, rendering them suitable for deployment in high-stakes settings. Additionally, our proposed method consistently outperforms existing learning techniques in terms of both model compactness and predictive accuracy. We further validate the computational efficiency of our proposed method by successfully training models using a reduced number of observations (order of a thousand) on both the urban driving and microsurgical datasets, allowing novice models to adapt their behavior effectively. We therefore represent our proposed method as an innovative paradigm for efficient imitation learning, capable of generating real-time adjustments to optimize both model performance and predictive accuracy in accordance with specific requirements. We therefore see the potential for our proposed method to effectively tackle a wide array of complex, high-stakes settings where model efficiency may be a greater concern than our current focus on environmental sensitivity. For instance, further research could involve designing compact models that minimize a patient's exposure to radiation during medical procedures or models that perfectly replicate the behavior of an experienced nurse while reducing the risk of needle sticks for patients. We therefore believe the proposed method has the potential to greatly impact various application domains

This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, thereby meeting the necessary phase condition for resonant precession.
Using a compact laser and mass-produced caesium vapour cell, it is possible to establish a highly sensitive field measurement device capable of reaching ultra-low field depths of several picotesla.
Our experimental caesium magnetometer, when applied in scientific research settings or as part of navigation systems, benefits from the introduction of digital maser feedback, thereby expanding the usable frequency range and allowing for more efficient operation. 

For optimal performance, our resonant maser system operates at a 2.48 MHz frequency, and further development could potentially adjust this frequency to match the 2.34 MHz transition of caesium-133 atoms more commonly used in clock systems, thereby providing a range of applications from both clockkeeping and measurement perspectives. 

Our results indicate that the enhanced performance of our system near the 2.48 MHz frequency suggests that digital maser feedback could serve as an efficient means of reaching the 2D maser configuration that caesium-133 clocks naturally reside in. 

This paper documents our experimental protocol and identifies potential advantages of integrating digital maser feedback into atomic clock systems. 

Our experiment demonstrates that the introduction of digital maser feedback facilitates the creation of a robust spin maser with robust performance characteristics, making it a viable solution for future clock systems. 

Our approach can be adapted for use in various systems of spin-polarized caesium-133 atoms, suggesting the potential for similar improvements to be implemented in systems of rubidium-87 and other alkali metals.

Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-mesh gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main issue with these detectors is identifying and eliminating background electron recoils triggered by gamma rays from radioactive substances within the detector and surroundings. We created new indicators that can tell electron and nuclear recoils apart at keV-level energies by using simulated ionization topologies. Our simulation shows that these indicators perform significantly better than the traditionally used dE/dx discriminant, offering up to three times greater differentiation. Additionally, these new indicators remain effective at lower ionization levels below 10 keV and remain resilient when the detector's direction-finding ability fails. We have also shown that these indicators can remain effective by simply adding an additional readout channel, allowing the tagging of recoil direction even when the primary direction is not known. We have provided mathematical explanations for how these indicators work and suggested methods to further improve their performance. Our study used simulations of mixtures with argon, such as Ar-He and Ar-Methane, and the results are independent of the specific mixture used. Our findings suggest that future large detectors, like the LUXE experiment, can identify nuclear recoils with high precision using these new indicators. Our study was conducted as part of the MaRTEr collaboration to explore the capabilities of future large-scale gas TPCs in recoil detection. These indicators are now being considered in future large-scale directional detector projects. A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors influencing driving behavior and designed a probabilistic framework to assess driver safety. The proposed method was then tested on real-world driver behavior data from Allens Wendy's contest in Argentina, utilizing experts from the company to provide contextual information. Compared to existing driver-assessment methods, our approach demonstrated enhanced effectiveness in predicting commercial driving behavior and more accurately reflected expert evaluation of driver safety. By considering context, our method produced more fair and consistent assessments of drivers. An evaluation experiment conducted online demonstrated that the proposed method's decision-making outcomes were preferable to those of behavior-based models from the perspective of both experts and non-experts. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those enhanced with OOV adaptations reveals a significant enhancement in detection accuracy, with increases ranging from 6% to 18% for various models on the holistic task.
The proposed methods are expected to have a positive impact on enhancing the versatility of deep learning-based OCR models to adapt to unseen text during real-world deployments. Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. To address this gap, researchers have recently employed topological data analysis, a leading method in the field. Notably, it was discovered that fields following Gaussian distributions form manifolds. Building on this discovery, this paper investigates the properties of geodesic curves within these Gaussian distributions. Specifically, we demonstrate that identifying geodesic curves is achievable although it's a computationally intensive task, requiring efficient strategies such as straying from the curve only by a margin of ε. Furthermore, we found that some geometric properties can be quantified more accurately than others, particularly those involving δ-regular points which can be approximated with high precision. On the other hand, it's computationally impractical to precisely determine ε-regular points. Our findings provide a framework for developing more accurate topological descriptors of these Gaussian distributions, such as covering sets and functions.
