One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering the PINNs as part of an iterative process that includes a posteriori error estimation, we aim to highlight the significance of utilizing known physical laws to guide data-driven methods. To achieve this, we apply PINNs to two nonlinear partial differential equations. The first example involves the Laplace equation, focusing on obtaining certified upper bounds for the errors made when using neural networks to approximate solutions. The results indicate that the error estimates are in good agreement with the actual errors made when adjusting the number of network parameters. The second example looks at the Burgers equation, aiming to demonstrate the potential of PINNs to provide a comprehensive outlook on the solution behavior by means of the Kolmogorov n-width. It is evident that the Kolmogorov n-width obtained from PINNs accurately predicts the actual n-width, showing that the PINNs can serve as highly accurate solutions. The proposed method also enables the determination of upper bounds for the errors made when using PINNs to approximate time-dependent PDEs. This is achieved by applying a posteriori error estimation to the temporal PINNs solution. Based on the observed results, it can be concluded that the use of PINNs has a positive impact on both training performance and the gain of insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. Furthermore, the method allows for validating the solution accuracy through error estimation. Future work may focus on extending the proposed approach to time-dependent PINNs that are informed by initial and boundary conditions in a more detailed manner. Moreover, it is interesting to incorporate the proposed technique into a iterative framework of physics-informed neural networks. This would allow for improving the solution quality by refining the training process. A possible direction is to develop a more sophisticated error estimation technique that can handle the constraints of PINNs in a more general setting. This would imply relaxing the requirements of the PINNs equations, allowing for the assessment of upper bounds for the errors made even when some of the PINNs equations are non-exact. Another potential area of improvement is a more systematic investigation into the actual computational costs associated with the use of PINNs, particularly in terms of training performance. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical measurement called the orbital magnetic moment, capable of being applied consistently across the entire range of the Brillouin zone.  Utilizing the orbital Hall effect offers the benefit of eliminating the subjective decision in setting the cut-off point for the indices involved in valley Hall conductivity, as the resulting conductivity in this new model becomes defined by an integral over the entire Brillouin zone of the orbital Berry curvature, an entirely new measurement.  Our new interpretation using OHE affords direct explanation for the accumulation of oppositely directed orbital moments observed on the edges of the sample in past Kerr rotation measurements.  Our theory further predicts an exponential decrease in the orbital magnetic field at larger gap sizes due to a break in symmetry in the bandgap, as well as an analysis of the orbital Hall effect in other types of two-dimensional materials with gaps.  Our investigation also reveals a relationship between the orbital Hall effect and a phenomenon called the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials, as well as a test using Raman spectroscopy to verify the presence of the orbital Hall effect. An experiment based on spin-Orbital coupling in a gapped graphene which is currently in the process of being conducted in the University of Konstanz, Germany will be able to verify the presence of the orbital Hall effect as well as provide an explanation for observed anomalies in past experiments. (To appear in Nature Communications)

We introduce three scenarios of data poisoning attacks on GNNs: a targeted attack intended to lower the model's accuracy, an unintended consequence of data poisoning where the model suffers from high accuracy, and an extensive poisoning of the entire graph dataset with no preferred outcome. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can enhance cross-matching capabilities, allowing for a more detailed examination. A new approach called Phot-astrometry Catalogue Matching combines a probability-based cross-match with the utilization of magnitude data. Through the analysis of a set of artificial sources, it was found that including magnitude details can boost cross-match efficiency by around 10%. To validate the efficacy of this method, the code participated in the third Gaia Cross-Matching Challenge, which focuses on matching sources between Gaia databases and various other catalogs. A comparison of the code's performance with that of established cross-match tools revealed that it ranked second among all participants, boasting the highest level of precision while maintaining high levels of accuracy and recall rates. Furthermore, the code demonstrated the ability to cross-match sources between Gaia databases and the 2MAPP catalog with a high degree of precision, outperforming other state-of-the-art tools like SQCAM and Palomar-Gaia cross-match. All necessary code and input files are publicly accessible through the developer's repository on GitHub. A set of demonstration videos illustrating the cross-match process and resulting outcomes are also available.

In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess property C(k, ρ) if the size of the intersection of all its sub-graphs of size k is less than ρ. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of vertices that intersects with every edge of the hypergraph. A vertex cover is considered minimal if none of its proper subsets serve as vertex covers. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. Notably, this visual innovation enables the associations of individual concepts to become apparent even when they are present in numbers as high as several thousand. Furthermore, OntoPlot provides an unparalleled capacity for efficient exploration and visualisation of reverse association sets that are crucial in identifying key properties and methods. The full OntoPlot suite, including a demonstration interface, is accessible online at http://onto-plot.com, complemented by a downloadable plugin for Cytoscope at http://cytoscape.org/. Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, can be downloaded at http://protege.stanford.edu/. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Our experimental findings on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal significant reductions in character error rate (approximately 8-8.5%), surpassing the baseline performance and exhibiting noticeable improvements on LibriSpeech test_clean. Notably, when applying the proposed method to LibriSpeech test_clean with 1000 hours of unsupervised data, we achieve a character error rate of 9.2%, outperforming a baseline model trained solely with supervised data. Additionally, using LibriSpeech test_clean with 800 hours of supervised data and 500 hours of unsupervised data, we observed a significant 16% character error rate reduction, further highlighting the benefits of the proposed approach. Our findings suggest that leveraging unpaired data with the proposed method significantly enhances end-to-end automatic speech recognition performance, even with extensive supervised data available. It is worth noting, however, that performance improvement diminishes with the amount of unsupervised data utilized. When using LibriSpeech test_clean with both 800 and 2000 hours of unsupervised data, the performance gain respectively amounts to 16% and 6%. Consequently, we anticipate that incorporating the proposed method will yield superior results in scenarios where access to abundant unsupervised data is limited. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. The employed approach views the robot's mental framework as a means of predicting the state of its surroundings and location on the navigation map. This prediction is then used to calculate the uncertainty associated with reaching the desired destination and, subsequently, guide the robot's movement. Experimental results indicate that this approach enables the robot to navigate through dynamic environments more effectively by reducing uncertainty. Additionally, these results suggest that the robot's mental framework can be utilized to identify and adapt to obstacles and that its predictive capabilities can be achieved through autonomous planning. This work has implications in various fields, including robotics, computer vision, and cognitive neuroscience. Moreover, this study highlights the potential of deep active inference as a promising technique for navigating complex environments. Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions. To isolate the effect of conformational changes, we softened the rigid molecules as well, yet found the outcome to be negligible, suggesting that the Soret effect in systems featuring internal degrees of freedom of the bulk components primarily relies on their energetic equivalence rather than their conformational balance. Conversely, the Soret effect in systems composed of two diverse substances appears to rely more heavily on the structural dissimilarity between flexible and rigid molecules, which in turn fosters greater asymmetry and results in strongly negative thermal diffusion coefficients, particularly at higher levels of stretching. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in unsupervised domain adaptive pedestrian detection.  Although current methods can integrate information from the source domain to achieve this, their approach is hampered by the inefficiency of self-attention mechanisms when dealing with high target domain densities, such as in urban settings.  We thus present a two-stage solution to overcome this challenge by leveraging source domain annotations more efficiently.  First, our method ranks candidate boxes according to their detection scores and source domain classifications.  Next, our enhanced box re-ranking process utilizes self-attention mechanisms to further evaluate each box, while reducing false positives by exploring nearest neighbors in the feature space.  This approach efficienly utilizes the vast amount of source domain data and requires no annotations from the target domain.  Experiments confirm that our method delivers the current best performance across multiple urban datasets worldwide, surpassing recent influential unsupervised domain adaptive pedestrian detection approaches. This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another converts synthetically created mel-spectrograms into high-quality audio waves that are perceptually natural-sounding. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses established methods, which apply more conventional techniques for reversing the mel-spectrogram process and another technique directly translating noisy audio waves to clear ones. Moreover, the research also examines the dependability of typical audio improvement evaluation metrics in the context of music by conducting a listening test. The study finds that the reliability of these metrics can be unreliable when evaluating music-specific quality. Consequently, the research proposes a new listening test setup and reliability scoring method, which can help gauge music enhancement quality more accurately. The study's code and listening test data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/jasegeb/imi. The research received partial funding from the Hong Kong Research Institute in eLearning.

Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings offer valuable insights for the development of more realistic and engaging artificial intelligence-powered throwing motions, particularly for applications such as computer graphics and virtual reality simulations. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages a tree-structured DRNN (Doubly-Recurrent Neural Networks) model originally proposed in 2017 by Alvarez-Melis and Jaakola. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential encoder with tree-structured decoding enhanced by a syntax-aware attention mechanism, differing from prior syntax-based NMT methods that rely on dependency parsing models. Conversely, the presented approach utilizes constituency parsing models, which it posits provides valuable information for translation. Moreover, by incorporating syntactic sentence structure, additional connections are established within the Seq2DRNN+SynC decoder neural network. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed Seq2DRNN architecture yields more natural translations and exhibits superior reordering abilities in comparison to sequential and state-of-the-art syntax-based NMT models. Consequently, it outperforms other models in both translation and constituency parsing tasks. Finally, the presented analysis offers insights into the capabilities of syntax-inspired NMT models. The proposed methodology is implemented into an open-source Python library available on GitHub.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective mechanisms to address the dual challenges of maintaining data reuse and learning a compressible representation through the establishment of two new algorithms, which demonstrate the empirical superiority and theoretical validity of their performance. Our analysis paves the way for the discovery of general principles in meta-learning. Additionally, we illustrate the practical significance of our findings by applying these principles to the realm of few-shot classification. Our work represents a significant step towards the confirmation of meta-learning's theoretical value. By creating algorithms that seamlessly integrate data from related tasks, we validate the empirical notions underlying meta-learning, thereby providing crucial theoretical insights to the field. Using a linear compression of the data distribution, we establish the theoretical efficacy of our representation learning methods, thereby providing concrete evidence of the efficacy of meta-learning. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing multilingual translation models, examining its efficacy in both translating and zero-shot scenarios. The results show that Distillation successfully reduces model size, surpassing quantitative performance after several post-processing interventions. Conversely, a thorough quantization process also achieves comparable performance levels with the original model, although at the expense of a greater training overhead. Based on these findings, the suggestion is made that Distillation should be the preferred approach for initializing a compressed model, but that a combination of both methods might be the best solution if a thorough training is feasible. The ultimate goal is to facilitate the creation of adaptable, low-resource language models that can also learn from multilingual datasets to improve their overall quality and efficiency. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain 3-uniform graphs, and discover that the Lagrangian density of the graph K-sub-2, when squared and multiplied by 4pi/3 and then taking the limit as the sub-2's order approaches infinity, results in an irrational number, providing the first example of an irrational Lagrangian density for a 3-uniform graph, and also showing that the conjecture is incorrect. Furthermore, our discovery suggests modifying the conjecture to state that all graphs with a Lagrangian density that can be expressed as a rational number plus the fraction of a square root plus a rational number have irrational Lagrangian density for a certain order of their subgraph, and we are unable to prove this modified conjecture. We leave the modified conjecture as an open problem. We also research and find the asymptotic rate of the maximum number of edges in K-sub-2, which is the first discovery of its kind. We leave the second problem as an open question, whether this can be discovered for all r-uniform graphs. The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of various sizes from a total dataset, each model undergoes a different image enhancement while its performance is compared to a baseline model trained without such augmentations on the entire dataset. Ultimately, we discovered that using rotate and mixup image enhancement methods leads to a significant reduction of 70% in labelled data requirements while demonstrating comparable results to the baseline in F-score classification and F-score score metrics. Additionally, combining these augmentations yields an even better performance, requiring only 125 images for training as opposed to the full dataset of 400 images for optimal F1 score. Therefore, we conclude that image enhancement techniques are a valuable tool in minimizing labelled data necessity for semantic segmentation tasks in medical image analysis. Hence, they can be utilized effectively to streamline the training of semantic segmentation deep learning models for specific tasks, such as pneumonia detection in chest X-rays. Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style and level of detail. This paper proposes a straightforward yet effective approach to adapting existing models for various captioning styles by utilizing prompts as adaptively tuned filters. By incorporating prompts into both the encoder and decoder of the model, the model can effectively produce captions in multiple styles. Unlike traditional techniques that require substantial training data, our approach can learn prompts using a minimal number of auxiliary images and even zero auxiliary images, essentially using the target domain data as the primary source of inspiration. Additionally, this paper explores the connection between prompts and data augmentation, allowing prompts to be learned using self-supervised methods. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can successfully achieve state-of-the-art performance on the COCO image captioning dataset without the need for extensive training. Furthermore, this paper's results highlight the intriguing relationship between prompts as filters and data augmentation, revealing that well-designed prompts can attain performance comparable to pretraining the encoder on the target domain, all while requiring significantly less data and effort. This discovery holds potential for other vision language tasks where finding optimal data augmentation can be a daunting and costly process. Lastly, this paper illustrates the potential of our approach by applying it to zero-shot image captioning, a more challenging task where both the input and output domains are unknown. This research was supported by the recent emergence of large-scale open-source datasets for image captioning, the significant growth of which has accelerated in recent years. Some key datasets employed in this research include:
* COCO-CAP dataset with 124K training captions
* COCO dataset with 121K images and 50K valid captions
* Visual Genome dataset with 3.4M captions
* CIDEr scores and the activations of the last encoder layer
* BLEU scores and the log-probability of the decoded caption given the input image features
* Fine-tuning the model on the COCO dataset for image captioning, using either the entire dataset or a small subset of data
* Zero-shot learning of the prompts using a few auxiliary images, rather than the entire dataset
* A decayed learning rate schedule for the prompts, similar to the one used for fine-tuning the model on the training data
* A deep decoder is beneficial for image captioning, allowing prompts to produce more detailed and coherent captions
* A decoupled training regime optimizes the objective function separately for the prompts and the pre-trained image feature extractor
* Data augmentation is an attractive source of extra supervision for learning prompts

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. We successfully implement zero-shot speech-to-text by first extracting speech features and translating them into text features, enabling the model to learn a joint text-to-text mapping. We also introduce a new form of data augmentation for speech data. Our models achieve impressive results, surpassing single-system and two-stage approaches on 20 new, unseen language pairs. Our work presents a novel approach to zero-shot speech-to-text, showcasing its promise in achieving high-quality outcomes with limited speech-to-text data, reducing the need for abundant text-to-text data, and minimizing the occurrence of inaccuracies. It also expands the capabilities of zero-shot translation to spoken languages. We publicly release our code and the newly created MuST-19 dataset containing 19 speech languages and written translations. The MuST-19 dataset fills a critical gap in the existing zero-shot translation literature and is an invaluable resource for the community. We also conduct a thorough error analysis, highlighting promising avenues for future research. While our work has made significant progress in zero-shot speech-to-text, there are still remaining challenges to address. We hope that our research will inspire future advancements in this area. The code for our work is maintained at https://github.com/jayelias/zero-shot-speech-to-text, while the MuST-19 dataset is hosted at https://must-dataset.github.io.

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain. Consequently, our study yields a broad class of scenarios where the interior and boundary processes are interdependent, while also facilitating scenarios where they function independently, including instances of Morrey-Campanato type. Moreover, our analysis yields a wide range of scenarios where the behavior of the system is essentially determined by its initial conditions, including cases of fading memory at the interior and boundary levels. Employing a novel approach based on the theory of strongly continuous solutions of abstract evolution equations, our study benefits from an exceptionally high level of flexibility in the generation function of the interior differential operator, the underlying structure of the boundary conditions, as well as the characteristics of the boundary conditions themselves. The study appears in its current form under conditions that are largely self-contained and accessible to a general audience. Nonetheless, additional research is foreseen, where it is intended to further explore well-posedness results associated with general evolution equations generated by operators with extensive applications across various fields. The work is intended to be part of a comprehensive series of studies that will be published in the future. The associated proof of the main theorem has been detailed in a separate document, which is meant to facilitate accessibility to this important section of research. The document can be accessed via the provided hyperlink. The approach to solving the system, as outlined in the proof, is intended to be utilized as a foundational model that can be adapted to address related systems with spatially varying coefficients, including cases with anisotropic properties. Furthermore, our research is designed to provide a potential starting point for exploring well-posedness results associated with diverse types of evolutionary equations, including those involving fractional differences and various types of memories. Ultimately, our approach is intended to be versatile and can be applied to a broad array of mathematical models describing physical processes at the microscopic and macroscopic levels. The related project is intended to further extend this approach to well-posedness results associated with a comprehensive category of evolutionary equations, including those involving fractional differences and various types of memories.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly distributed and irregular load patterns. Although existing probabilistic forecasting methods offer valuable uncertainty assessment for a single, specific load profile, they typically fail to account for the possible peak loads that may occur. To address this limitation, this study proposes a new approach consisting of two parts: the dynamic linear model, which generates probabilistic forecasts for typical and peak loads, and the "fusion" technique, which combines these forecasts with actual peak load observations to produce more accurate and refined point forecasts. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this model and this "fusion" technique by analyzing and evaluating forecasts for Italian low voltage nodes, using data from the CEC SANDIA consortium. Our study reveals that point forecasts generated by this technique tend to be more accurate and refined than those produced by other established probabilistic models, and ultimately more reliable load predictions are achieved. Furthermore, this study also finds that "fusion" technique leads to significant improvements of around 15% to even 20% in the RMSE score for specific forecast timeframes. Our research highlights the value of an additional peak load forecast that can be obtained with the help of this "fusion" technique, and we find that this additional peak load forecast enables about 50% reduction in the RMSE score, and in the same time the CRP score is significantly improved too. On the other hand, the effectiveness of the dynamic model and the "fusion" technique also emerges when the forecasts are evaluated in terms of the CRPS score, and it is revealed that the "fusion" technique leads to significant improvements of around 60% to even 70% in the CRPS score for specific forecast timeframes. Finally, our research also finds that the "fusion" technique leads to significant reductions of around 30% to even 40% in the CRPS score for specific forecast timeframes, and this outcome is attributed to an enhanced uncertainty assessment and refined forecasts that can be obtained with the help of this "fusion" technique. In summary, our research confirms that probabilistic forecasting and "fusion" techniques are effective and reliable methods that can be employed to manage and forecast the intricate low voltage load profiles, and our study provides valuable insights that could be applied to a wide range of forecasting tasks, and these could be particularly useful in a smart grid setting. Creating a reliable model to precisely identify COVID-19 signs in chest CT scans despite limited labelled data is essential due to the current shortage of such resources. A new two-stage framework is proposed, using weakly supervised ideas, to accurately detect and segment COVID-19 lesions in such scans. Stage 1 uses a new loss function and an existing model to optimise feature extraction, then associate these features with individual lesions through $k$-means clustering. Stage 2 employs a novel lesion-level model and adaptive tri-class active learning strategy to accurately determine the type and location of these individual lesions. Experiments using two separate datasets confirm the framework's ability to accurately detect and segment COVID-19 lesions. The framework produced results comparable to those of fully supervised methods, even in the presence of noisy labels. Furthermore, its adaptive tri-class active learning strategy significantly reduces the required number of labels needed. The framework outperforms existing solutions, including fully supervised and unsupervised approaches, according to recent competitions results. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the exceptional performance of 97.6% in identifying the correct vertebrae and 96.7% in accurately counting their number. Notably, the method demonstrated superior performance in various scenarios, such as vertebral compression fractures, post-operative cases, and CT scans with metallic streak artifacts, exhibiting great potential for the automatic analysis of complex spine disorders. The proposed method has been successfully tested using open-source technologies such as PyTorch, numpy, and torchvision, which are highly recommend for further research purposes. These features, along with the cavity's influence on the system, are to be identified in experimental setups involving ultrastrong light-matter coupling. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in Hilbert-Schmidt distance. Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also simulate the implementation of these algorithms on noisy quantum devices, modeling them as linear combinations of perfect circuits to quantify the effect of noise on the separation test. Our results indicate that the VSV's performance closely matches the performance of its state-model counterpart when executed within realistic error tolerances. Notably, we discover that in certain cases, the cost function is not sufficiently convex to ensure unique solutions for large numbers of qubits. Nonetheless, the VSV's ability to handle complex systems is demonstrated, and we suggest potential enhancements to enhance its convexity. Our research explores an alternative cost function that better facilitates resource-efficient implementation. Our results suggest that the VSV's performance can be significantly improved by simply eliminating a non-diagonal component of the cost function. This enables the use of the stochastic gradient descent technique, significantly reducing the number of expensive state vector computations required. Our experiments demonstrate that this modification effectively facilitates efficient verification of separability in complex quantum systems with minimal overhead. A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images after selecting a target item. Although advancements have been made, the task remains challenging due to the need for extensive data labeling and the lack of methods for manipulating image features. This study focuses on semi-supervised feature-level attribute manipulation for fashion image retrieval, and the main contributions are as follows: First, we introduced a framework for attribute manipulation that can modify a query image's features while maintaining its visual appearance. This approach was then combined with an existing retrieval model, which uses a neural network to predict whether two images share the same attributes. Experimental results revealed that our proposed framework significantly improves the performance of the retrieval model, and in return, enhances overall image retrieval performance. Two key components enabled this success: first, we modified a style transfer model to preserve more features, including colors and subtle textures; second, we developed a novel objective function for our framework that maximizes the correlation between manipulated images and the target attributes. This objective function addresses the challenging task of manipulating image features while maintaining attribute consistency. This challenge is even more pronounced in fashion image retrieval, which involves retrieving images of the same item or with compatible attributes. When applying our framework to fashion image retrieval, we observed a notable increase in retrieval accuracy, which in turn improved the overall image retrieval performance. Our study also sheds light on the importance of image features in fashion image retrieval. When evaluating the proposed framework using multiple metrics, we found that it generalizes well to other datasets, including those for cars and cells. This study provides an essential step towards solving the challenging task of fashion instance-level image retrieval. While our proposed framework addresses one aspect of this task, it does not fully solve the problem. For instance, we found that the proposed framework can cause some feature-level attribute manipulations to be perceptibly distorted, which may hinder its potential to improve the overall image retrieval performance. A future study will focus on addressing these distortions to further improve the image retrieval results. In summary, this study contributes towards solving the challenging task of fashion instance-level image retrieval by introducing a semi-supervised feature-level attribute manipulation approach that has been evaluated using multiple criteria and demonstrated promising success. This research has the potential to influence various applications that rely on image retrieval, including fashion design, recommendation systems, and related business applications. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process intricate and labor-intensive. This paper proposes a novel cost constructor, designed with convolutional neural networks, to simplify the process and make it more efficient. Our constructor, leveraging a pre-trained network, can automatically generate a cost map from a light field, outperforming the existing sequential shifting method and setting a new benchmark for depth estimation in light fields. Furthermore, our proposed constructor can effectively handle occlusions by using a structured patch embedding approach, yielding substantial improvements in cases of heavy occlusions. Experiments conducted on public datasets prove our approach to be more efficient and effective than existing methods, paving the way for future research on the estimation of light field depth. The source code of our approach can be found on the GitHub repository 'OFDE_Occupational'.

However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three notable examples – Torsional gravity, Simple Symmetric Gravity, and Cardy-Bonelli gravity – within double field theory and derives their corresponding action frameworks. What's more, double field theory's framework also enables the creation of novel action frameworks for these theories that were previously unexplored. This note details the procedure for doing so and includes a case study involving 2-dimensional gravity. Overall, double field theory's versatility in describing extra dimensions lends itself as an ideal tool for developing these alternative gravity theories. This tool allows for a direct connection between the geometric structure of the target space (in this case, a three-dimensional space of constant curvature) and the accompanying branch of double field theory. As an added benefit, double field theory's framework also facilitates the creation of gauge fields with a non-constant gradient on the target space. This field plays a vital role in describing the dynamics of the alternative gravity theories in question. Finally, the note concludes with a case study involving higher-dimensional gravity and explores the potential application of double field theory in the field of gravity research.
